title: Longline fishery in a marine reserve – catching protected megafauna in the Galapagos Islands
abstract_text: Marine megafauna (elasmobranchs, mammals, turtles, birds) is important from an ecological point of view because it occupies upper trophic levels and is also often essential for marine tourism. Species belonging to this group are often heavily impacted by fishing due to their longevity, late sexual maturity and low reproductive output, which affect the capability to recover from depletion. In the Galapagos, marine megafauna is protected throughout the marine reserve and is the main attraction for marine tourism, generating millions of dollars in revenue annually. Multiple artisanal longlining projects were carried out since the 1990s with the aim of redirecting fishing effort from the depleted coastal-demersal species to pelagic fish, such as yellowfin tuna, Thunnus albacares and swordfish, Xiphias gladius. All these projects have resulted in high bycatch of megafauna. Despite its importance in the archipelago, megafauna is still being caught as bycatch in the longline fishery, without independent scientific studies to evaluate its impact, largely due to poor objective definition, data collection, and enforcement. To fill in this knowledge gap, we analyzed data of the fifth longline fishing project (2012-2013) to describe the fishery, identify variables affecting bycatch, and suggest mitigation strategies. This experimental project involved twelve fishing vessels, which deployed 42,007 hooks catching 4,893 individuals belonging to 33 species, mostly yellowfin tuna. Of those, 16 species were protected megafauna, particularly blacktip sharks, Carcharhinus limbatus and oceanic manta, Manta birostris. These species were regularly captured during the two fishing seasons and in all the four bioregions that occur in the archipelago, suggesting little potential to mitigate their catch. As an alternative, we identified 14 hotspots where yellowfin tuna and swordfish could be harvested through more selective fishing techniques. In an archipelago where the main economic activity is marine wildlife tourism, the implementation of an extractive and unselective activity such as pelagic longline fishing should be avoided to ensure the preservation of the Galapagos marine ecosystem and its booming tourism industry.

title: Using local ecological knowledge to reconstruct trends in elasmobranch populations in the Strait of Sicily
abstract_text: Fishers have a rich knowledge of the resources and the environment in which they work, that is rarely utilised to provide advice on the status of exploited populations. Fishers "local ecological knowledge" (LEK) can be used to reconstruct species trends, like sharks, that currently are at very low biomass due to overfishing. In this study we used the historical memories of Sicilian fishers to gather data on change in fishing practices and capture of cartilaginous species in the Strait of Sicily over the last decades. We conducted interviews with 27 retired trawl fishers from Mazara del Vallo harbour (SW Sicily) using a pre-defined questionnaire with a series of open and fixed questions and comparing to the present abundance. The questionnaire included specific questions about the trends they perceived in cartilaginous fish occurence abundance between 1940s and 2000s (according to three main time periods 1940-1960, 1961-1980 and 1981-2010), in order to facilitate the estimation of eventual changes over time. A total of 29 species were mentioned by fishermen during interviews, including large pelagic sharks (Carcharhinidae, Sphyrnidae and Lamnidae), mesopredatory demersal sharks (Squalidae, Hexanchidae, Centrophoridae, Oxynotidae, Triakidae, Scyliorhinidae and Squatinidae) and batoids. Overall shark catches were perceived to have diminished since the early 1940s: about 95% of fishers reported the decline of commercially important species (e.g. Mustelus spp.) and indicated species that could have been depleted (e.g. Squatina spp., Sphyrna spp.). Our study shows that LEK of fishers can be beneficial for reconstructing long-term population trends of exploited species when traditional standard data on fisheries catch or species relative abundance from surveys is limited or only available for recent periods. The results obtained cleary indicate the rapid and alarming decline of elasmobranchs in the Strait of Sicily highlighting the need for urgent conservation measures to be adopted.

title: Molecular identification of endangered marine predators by barcoding ancient museum rostra of Mediterranean sawfish populations
abstract_text: A growing concern in conserving threatened animals affected by human impact has been significant worldwide. Among marine animals, sawfishes (Chondrichthyes, Pristidae) are considered one of the most endangered families among elasmobranchs, resulting in extinction in many coastal areas around the world, including the Mediterranean Sea. Here, sawfish occurred with two species, Pristis pristis and P. pectinata, until the second half of the last century and are now considered Critically Endangered/Possibly Extinct. The historical occurrence of sawfish in the area is documented by bibliographic/ archival records and numerous preserved historical rostra available in museum collections. In this study we attempted to genetically characterize the historical remains of sawfish from several European museums and to enable, in the future, the preliminary investigation of their evolutionary and ecological relationships with global samples. A total of 80 rostra specimens, dated from 1813 to 1959 and catalogued as unknown origin or Mediterranean (11), were collected from 11 European museums and were properly prepared for ancient DNA genetic analysis. Taxonomic identification at the species level was obtained through PCR amplification of small fragments (150 bp) of two mitochondrial markers commonly used for species identification (i.e., the mitochondrial COI and the NADH2). Sequence comparison with currently available ones from public repositories and phylogenetic tree analyses indicated that the historical specimens belonged to four species, P. pristis, P. zijsron, P. pectinata, and Anoxypristis cuspidata, with a high frequency of mismatches (69%) between molecular identification and species museum cataloguing, when present. These preliminary data also showed the presence of two sequence sub-clusters in the poorly barcoded species P. zijsron. With the expansion of this initial analysis, we will contribute to increase the limited molecular data of these critically endangered large predators and to exploit historical genetic data for reconstructing phylogenetic/phylogeographic extent of the possibly extinct population of Mediterranean sawfish.

title: Involving stakeholders in the evaluation of Atlantic shark fisheries management strategies and why they matter to sharks
abstract_text: Shortfin-mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) and blue shark (Prionace glauca) are the two most captured pelagic shark species in the Atlantic Ocean. Since 1990 Spanish longline fleet has been registered for the highest by-cacth of both species in the Atlantic Ocean. About shortfin-mako, concern has been raised after the last evaluation for the northern Atlantic in 2017 made by ICCAT and the stock assessment update meeting held in 2019. It stated the population being overfished and suffering from overfishing. About blue shark, although capture levels appear to be within sustainable fishing limits, it is subject to high exploitation rates in the Atlantic. Uncertainties in assessment results suggest that additional management actions could be considered for both species. In this study different fisheries management strategies were evaluated for shortfin-mako and blue shark in the Atlantic from the stakeholder’s perspective. Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK) was considered to be useful as fishermen possess a unique knowledge based on their continued interaction with the species and the environment. Information was collected through personal interviews with fishermen from the Spanish longline fleet and surveys sent out to scientists and NGOs. Interviews allowed to collect fishermen’s observations on variations of abundance, distribution patterns, size of capture and seasonal fluctuations for both species. SWOT-analysis was used to study the different factors to be taken into account for various management measures. Main management strategies proposed by stakeholders were time-area closure, especially for blue shark juveniles during the summer months in the Sole Bank, minimum capture size and a quota system. This study suggests that management could be supported by involving stakeholders due to their knowledge about the species and environment. Lastly, observations of fishermen about ecological features of both species could be used as a valid aid for future scientific studies.

title: SharkPulse: taking the pulse of global shark populations
abstract_text: Many species of sharks and their relatives are declining worldwide at a rapid rate because of their vulnerable life histories exposed to impacts of fishing and habitat modification. For this reason, they are among the most endangered animals in the ocean. Meanwhile, they are also the most poorly quantified groups of animals in the ocean as basic information on abundance and distribution is lacking for about half of their species. Lack of data is hampering conservation assessment and policy actions and has thus become one of the biggest issues for shark conservation. Available solutions for developing effective conservation actions and reverse loss include exploring alternative sources of information and unconventional methods to collect and analyze abundance and distribution data. Here we show how to transition from data deficient to big data for many shark species. By taking advance of the surge of information on human ocean use and communication, we show how crowdsourcing, web data-mining and machine learning can fill this critical information gap. We integrated these approaches in a modular crowd-sourcing platform that combines social network and web site crawling, web applications, smartphone technology, and image analysis to build the largest database of shark sighting available today. We will show how these data can be used to produce species distribution and models to inform conservation assessments and promote protection and recovery plans.

title: Spatial variability of Chondrichthyes in the North Mediterranean
abstract_text: Thanks to the availability of the MEDITS survey data, a picture of the occurrence, abundance and distribution of Chondrichthyes in the Mediterranean basin was done. During the spring-summer MEDITS period (2012-2015), 41 Chondrichthyes, including 18 sharks (5 Orders and 10 Families), 22 batoids (3 Orders and 4 Families) and 1 chimaera, were detected from several Geographical Subareas (GSAs). In general, it is possible to observe that batoid species had a preferential distribution in the shelf (10-200 m) while “shark” species were more frequent in the slope (200-800 m). Only three species, the Carcharhiniformes Galeus melastomus, Scyliorhinus canicula and the Torpediniformes Torpedo marmorata were caught in all several GSAs studied. On the shelf, the Rajidae family was represented in primis by Raja clavata and then by R. miraletus, R. polystigma and R. asterias. The slope was characterized by the prevalence of the blackmouth catshark G. melastomus in all GSAs followed by S. canicula, E. spinax and Squalus blainville. Throughout a comparison between the maps of trawling fishing pressure in Mediterranean (Sbrana et al., 2013) and our maps of abundance’s species it is clear that the most affected areas, as Adriatic sea and Spanish areas (with the exception of the Baleares islands) registered low abundance of Elasmobranchs but other areas with high level of pressure, as the South western of Sicily, presented high level of abundance, showing that, in this case, other environmental drivers work together with the fishing pressure to define the levels of biomass and density. Results of Generalized Additive Models (GAM) highlighted the depth range (followed by the temperature) as one of the most important drivers influencing the distribution of both batoid and shark species.

title: “Winners & Losers”, a vulnerability analysis of sharks, rays and chimaeras in the Gulf of California (GoC), Mexico
abstract_text: Fisheries contribute to food security and poverty alleviation, particularly in developing countries such as Mexico. Therefore, it is important to assess the risks to fisheries resources in a comprehensive way. The vulnerability analysis of 106 species of pelagic, coastal and demersal chondrichthyans in the Gulf of California area performed in this study involves two regions (the southern and entrance), two timescales (2050 and 2099), four types of fishing and eight climate change stressors. The risk from fishing stressors is related to exposure to the demersal prawn fishery, the artisanal fishery, the industrial shark fishery, and the sardine fishery from 2006 to 2017, also depending on the species’ productivity and susceptibility. The risk from climate change stressors was assessed by how species are likely to be affected by eight climate change stressors (rising water temperature, increasing storm frequency and intensity, changing currents and upwelling, increasing salinity, decreasing DO and chlorophyll-a and increasing ocean acidity). The assessment was based on the species’ sensitivity and adaptability to changing habitats and on indicators of what may happen based on IPCC emissions scenarios for the area by 2100. We have assessed which species of chondrichthyans are likely to be highly affected (“Losers”) and those considered “Winners” by assigning each species to six ecological groups (EGs) (a novel and flexible way to allocate a great number of species) based on species’ lifestyle and habitat. The EGs of shelf-inshore, shelf-reef and shelf-sand (≤75 m) are likely to have high exposure risk to the climate change stressors under medium and high emission scenarios, whereas exposure risk from fishing stressors was high for the EGs of shelf-inshore and shelf-sand (≤75 m) in both regions.

title: Toxic soup: Fins from top traded shark species in Hong Kong and China found not recommended for human consumption
abstract_text: The trade of shark-derived products is a primary driver of the decline in shark populations globally. Shark fin is one of China’s top dried seafood products and, with over 80 shark species currently present in the Hong Kong (HK) trade, shark fin soup is an asian delicacy on high demand. The high position of sharks in marine food webs and their relatively long life spans mean that they can often have high concentrations of heavy metals in their tissues. Heavy metals including mercury (Hg), Methylmercury (MeHg), lead (Pb), arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd) and selenium (Se) all have adverse health effects on humans, especially in pregnant women and children. Shark meat contains high values of Hg, often surpassing the recommended human consumption advisory limits. To date, little is known about the risks of consuming shark fin products on a regular basis, and virtually no studies have addressed this issue. Here, we analyze processed shark fins from the China and HK markets (n=267) for Hg, MeHg, Pb, As, Cd and Se to obtain novel information on their heavy metal concentrations and to inform consumers of the risks of ingesting fins from a suite of species (n=9) currently heavily traded. Results indicate all shark species in the study are above maximum consumption Hg limits established by HK and US EPA. A complex of Blacktip species, Carcharhinus longimanus, Prionace glauca, Sphyrna lewini and Sphyrna Zygaena all surpass the European comission’s Hg limits (1ppm) and WHO/JECFA’s MeHg potential tolerable weekly intake (1.6 𝜇gMeHg/kg bw). P. glauca samples were found to surpass inorganic As maximum levels established by WHO/JECFA (70.59% samples > 3 𝜇giAs/kg bw ). Results show high inter and intra-specific variation in Hg, As and MeHg concentrations, as well as low Cd, Se and Pb concentrations for the majority of individuals.

title: Baselines for butterfly babies: towards a mediteranean study model
abstract_text: The spiny butterfly ray, Gymnura altavela, is a benthic batoid found on soft bottoms in shallow coastal waters in the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, where it is considered a Critically Endangered species on certain areas of its distribution. As G. altavela is a species with a patchy and discontinuous distribution, the identification, characterization and protection of its congregation areas may be the key issue for the future of the species. Its big size, calmed behaviour and presence in beaches with a high tourist activity make this species an emblematic animal for conservation plans. To evaluate this purpose, a series of monthly surveys were conducted during a year in areas located in Alicante (South-Eastern Spain) with different level of tourism. In each survey, the number of spiny butterfly ray marks found in the sediment with its length, width and location depth were recorded. Live animals found were also measured in length and width, and pictures of the pectoral fins and tail were taken for photoidentification. A total of 26 different alive animals were found during the daily surveys, showing a disc width range of 77-112 cm for males and 53-157 cm for females. The alive specimens found were resting on the bottom covered by sediment beside seagrass meadows of Posidonia oceanica or Cymodocea nodosa. Only juvenile specimens (<64 cm width) were found resting in sand patches within C. nodosa meadows. The occurrence of females was constant throughout the year, while male occurrence was higher in spring. During the period October-June, coinciding with the months of less tourism, spiny butterfly ray specimens and its marks were observed in all the surveyed areas, whereas during June-September period, coinciding with the tourism season, no animals or its marks could be observed in the areas with high level of tourism activities.

title: The development of a long-standing citizen science project: the Great Eggcase Hunt
abstract_text: As a long-standing citizen science project of the Shark Trust, the Great Eggcase Hunt (GEH) has received nearly a quarter of a million records to date. Initially developed to engage the public in shark conservation and to find out more about the diversity and broad distribution of oviparous elasmobranchs in British waters, the GEH now regularly receives records from around the world, including as far afield as Ecuador. Surprisingly little is known about the distribution and habitat of the spawning and nursery areas of skate and oviparous sharks, and the eggcases of many species have yet to be described. Citizen science engagement can support broader scientific initiatives in areas where data may be otherwise limited and can strengthen inferences made on important habitats. Data obtained from the project so far has allowed us to detail the morphological characteristics of 13 species found around the British Isles, with an additional paper on the distribution of juvenile stages and eggcases of skate in prep. Collaborations with partner organisations - the Dutch Shark Society (Netherlands) and APECE (Portugal) - and the translation of the GEH smartphone app into the corresponding languages has allowed the reach and scope of the project to broaden. The increased accessibility of GEH identification and recording materials has resulted in improved accuracy of submissions of spent eggcases, an increase in submissions of in-situ sightings, and from fish markets, scientific trawls and commercial fisheries. Photographic capabilities within the app have enabled more records to be verified to species level. As the Trust continues to develop the GEH and make it more accessible internationally, our objective is to expand on the existing species-specific knowledge of oviparous elasmobranchs. As a result, this could help inform on the nominal distribution of egg-laying grounds and potentially aid conservation measures on a local and international level.

title: Preliminary evidences of illegal elasmobranch fishing in Libya
abstract_text: Social media networks are emerging as an important additional tool for monitoring wildlife especially in areas with low data availability. Libya is located in the central Mediterranean and is considered a data scarce area regarding its marine biodiversity. Few information is also available about elasmobranch species, however this country has been recently identified among the top priority countries for elasmobranch conservation with low conservation likelihood and yet high fisheries pressure. For this work, in the context of an ongoing project, we performed a rapid assessment on social media for detecting elasmobranch occurrences from Libya. A total of 55 records of elasmobranch occurrences collected, with the vast majority (93.73%) resulting from (professional and recreational) fishing activity, while the rest were observations of divers and marine users. All records identified to the species level resulting in fifteen different species but one observation was recorded as Squatina sp. as the identification to the species level was not possible. Carcharhinus plumbeus (≈16%), Glaucostegus cemiculus (≈14%), Squatina squatina (≈10%) and Rhinobatos rhinobatos (≈10%) were the most commonly posted species. The vast majority of the observation depicted fished individuals of which ≈78% species listed Endangered or Critically Endangered in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, while ≈60% were species protected by the Barcelona Convention and consequently Recommendation GFCM/42/2018/2 (amending GFCM/36/2012/3); in both cases, Libya is a signatory party. This is a very first step on a long-term project that aims to understand the elasmobranch diversity in Libya and bring into light information about their fishing and trade. Hereby we present the first data collected through the social media network FacebookTM, however in the near future further observation will be collected and findings will be complemented with fish and auction market surveys and questionnaires to all relevant stakeholders.

title: Putting the spotlight on Mediterranean angel sharks
abstract_text: Angel sharks (Squatinidae) are considered one of the most threatened Families of chondrichthyans in the world. Of the 22 species, three are present in the Mediterranean – Sawback Angelshark Squatina aculeata, Smoothback Angelshark S. oculata, and Angelshark S. squatina – all three are Critically Endangered. Population sizes and geographic ranges of these species have declined primarily due to overfishing and habitat loss. With angel sharks now rarely encountered, reliance falls on fisheries data, reports of incidental catch, citizen science, social media, and interviews with fishers to increase knowledge on distribution. The Mediterranean has revealed itself to be a hotspot of extinction risk for chondrichthyans. In 2012, the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) banned the retention of 24 species of exceptionally threatened elasmobranchs, including the three species of angel sharks. Although protected on paper, these species remain exposed to fisheries pressure by those coastal states yet to act on their commitments. The complex and multijurisdictional nature of the Mediterranean (with >20 coastal states and territories) creates a need for collaborative action to build capacity for angel shark conservation. Drawing on the expertise of the Angel Shark Conservation Network, a group of regional experts were brought together in Tunisia (in March 2019) to begin development of a Regional Action Plan for these imperiled species. The Action Plan outlines key threats, goals, objectives, and actions needed to achieve the vision that: Mediterranean angel sharks are restored to robust populations, fulfilling their ecological roles in healthy ecosystems. This work follows on from the development of the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Angel Shark Conservation Strategy which provides a framework for improved protection, guiding future research, management, policy and conservation actions.

title: High levels of mislabeling in elasmobranch meat products – Investigating species utilisation with DNA barcoding in the Mediterranean
abstract_text: Food authenticity has received an increasing focus due to high profile cases of mislabeling, with increasing numbers of investigations identifying sales of endangered or prohibited species that were illegally caught or landed under international and/or national legislation. A total of 160 shark products (steaks or fillets) were examined from fishmongers and markets across Greece and Italy from over a decade. Both countries follow food and safety legislation regarding elasmobranch meat sales, which require specific commerial designation on labels - “Galeos” and “Palombo” for Greece and Italy that are restricted to only Mustelus spp.. The barcode (a partial sequence of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I gene, COI) was used to analyze samples, and species were identified by reference to genetic databases (BOLD and GenBank). The results revealed differences in patterns of species utilisation between countries, with Italy showing a higher level of mislabeling and prohibited species in sales. About three quarter of products (73.75%) originated from species that are locally listed as threatened by the IUCN red list (vulnerable, endangered and critically endangered). The mislabeled products represent 57.76% of all sales, and of them, 47.31% originated from species with current prohibitions on landings or CITES listings. This includes large sharks (i.e. H. griseus, H. perlo, A. vulpinus) that bear little resemblance to Mustelus spp. and likely demonstrate deliberate substitution. Mislabeled products are providing a route for prohibited and protected sharks to enter the food supply chain and be sold to consumers who are misguided and unaware they are purchasing endangered species.

title: School shark (Galeorhinus galeus) stock assessment off the Algerian coast
abstract_text: Galeorhinus galeus (Linnaeus, 1758) is a demersal shark, belonging to the Galeomorphii superorder and the Triakidae family. A follow-up, carried out in the late nineties, allowed to establish the total length frequencies distributions of 414 individuals. The analysis of size structures allowed determining the growth and exploitation parameters required by the Thompson and Bell model (1934). This model designed for the length-based analysis, evaluates the impact of a variation in fishing effort with mesh change effect in short and long-term catch forecasts. Input data are provided by the Jones technique (1983), which, by pseudo-cohort analysis (VPA), determines mortality coefficients. Changes in fishing mortality F (VPA) show that the smallest classes are the least fished (low F values). Juveniles are not vulnerable to exploitation; this phenomenon partly assures the state of the stock, but do not overshadow the fishing pressure suffered by the parents. Such observation reflects an overexploitation situation, recruitment type. The Thompson and Bell model calculates F-factors and corresponding biomass, Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) and Maximum Sustainable Economic Yield (MSEY). It suggests increasing the current fishing effort at least three times without any collapse risk for the population but without appreciable production gain. This analysis put the last touches on the hypothesis given by the cohort analysis. The results reflect a high vulnerability of the school shark due to its occurrence on the different biotopes. In order to the stock for sustainability, the effort must be transferred to other sea bottoms and reduce current individuals size to 130-140 cm of total length. It is therefore necessary to gather ecological information, for the analysis risks of this stock. While hoping an implementation of policies for catch and bycatch of vulnerable sharks in the whole Mediterranean.

title: Mako Sharks: overfished yet overlooked. Exploring the latest advice & management opportunities
abstract_text: The Shortfin Mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) is the world’s fastest shark, and sought for its meat, fins and sport. Overfished and overlooked by fisheries managers for decades, North Atlantic mako are now on the brink of population collapse. Since 2004 Scientific advisors to the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) have warned that the stock was overfished, that overfishing was likely, and that the South Atlantic stock was likely fully exploited. Subsequent ICCAT stock assessments culminated in stark advice in 2017. With evidence for the North Atlantic showing a 90% probability that the stock is overfished and experiencing overfishing, ICCAT scientists recommended the most effective immediate measure: a complete prohibition of retention. Yet despite the clarity of scientific advice Parties to ICCAT adopted a Recommendation which did not cap landings and has failed to stop overfishing. To this day mako sharks remain a No Limits species in high-seas fisheries. In 2019 several publications have furthered the understanding of the plight of mako sharks: updated projections and new scientific advice from ICCAT reinforcing the severity of the population decline; publication of an IUCN Red List reassessment recognising Shortfin Mako as now globally Endangered; and listing proposals for Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) (result pending at the time of writing). In the context that the fleets from the European Union (EU) take more makos than any other ICCAT Party - and with the EU a cosponsor of the 2019 CITES Appendix II listing proposal - this talk will explore the pressing need for management for makos (with an empahisis on the actions of the EU), and consider the opportuntiies for complimentarity between Wildlife Treaties such as CITES and the Regional Fisheries Management Organisations such as ICCAT.

title: A roadmap for interesting and effective shark research communication on social media
abstract_text: Part of the job as a researcher is to communicate research with the public and make information accessible, but how to do it efficiently can be a challenge. Social media is a great platform for reaching a large amount of people and if handled correctly it can be a very efficient communication tool. There is also a value in being mentioned and talked about by utilizing social media as well as legacy mass communication channels to enrich information exchanges between the scientific community and public audiences about elasmobranch. By using social media effectively for outreach such as interactions with reporters/newspapers and activly participating in discussion on social media, can assist the researchers field by promoting his/her scientific impact. My thesis and guidelines is a great startingpoint for any researcher that wants to use social media for elasmobranch communication. The communication guidelines I created in my Bachelor are based on social media studies, marketing strategies and my own thesis. The Institute of Marine Research used these guidelines in a communication project, to get public citizens to report sightings of basking sharks in Norwegian waters. The basking shark has become a rare sight due to overfishing/low reproductive rate. Due to the rarity of the shark in Norwegian waters it was important that we reached a broad audience. Through The Institute of Marine Research communication channels on social media and traditional outlets such as newspapers/radio our reach went farther than expected and we had an overwhelming positive feedback from the public with a 33% increase of yearly reported observations. From 37 reports over five years, to 21 reports in 1 month. Ultimately this study demonstrates that our communication strategy and social media guidelines are an effective way of research communication and this contribution may be especially relevant for scientists using social media for elasmobranch research communication.

title: Data Collection and Conservation Campaign for Sawfishes (Pristidae) in Indonesia
abstract_text: Sawfishes (Pristidae) are one of the most rare and endangered rays that deserve urgent global initiative to conserve them. Indonesia has issued regulation to prevent the extinction of the species i.e. Government Decree no. 7 in 1999. However, recent evidences stated that the fishing (targeted and by-catch) still occurred across the Indonesian waters. This paper aims to share the experience on developing data collection framework and conservation campaign entirely dedicated to preserve these species. In 2017, INDONESAW, an international collaborative project, has been established to address these conservation issues. Specific social media and communication material were produced and published. Additionally a network of seven focal points was selected and trained in order to perform sensitization data collection and community education of this charismatic species. The challenges to deal with ecological and socio-economic aspects as well as recommendations are discussed in this paper.

title: Stars Aligning. Studying the sharks of the Saba Bank, a bidoveristy hotspot in the Dutch Caribbean
abstract_text: We present on an international expedition for shark research to the Saba Bank in the Dutch Caribbean organised by the Dutch Elasmobranch Society (NEV), the Saba Conservation Foundation (SCF) and the Nature Foundation Sint Maarten (NFSM) in July 2019. The Saba Bank is the largest submarine atol in the Atlantic Ocean approximatelely 60km long and 40km wide. The atol is a hotspot for marine biodiversity with high coral coverage and abundant fish populations. Only limited research has been done on the elasmobranchs in the area. This is why the overall goal of the research expedition was to gain insight into the role the Saba Bank plays in the life cycle of the elasmobranch species that come there within Wider Caribbean region. The research focussed on: Tagging tigers: We tested a new satellite tag technology developed by the European Space Agency that will allow battery life of tags to extend well beyond what the current tag technology can do, and at a fraction of the cost. Nurse shark bycatch: Working with the local fishermen on reducing bycatch of nurse sharks in lobster traps. Part of this research is learning more about the behaviour of the sharks in and around the traps. Mote Marine lab have developed a video system that can be used to register shark behaviour. Shark connectivity and population genetics: Stable isotope analysis combined with an existing acustic telemetry array to learn more about the connectivity between different areas and the way these species use the Saba Bank. This will be combined with a close kin genetics study to help estimate population size. Stress levels in captured sharks: Taking blood samples (lactate, Ph) of captured animals to assess their welfare when handled on board.

title: Abundance and distribution of the white shark in the Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: Conservation of apex predators is a key challenge both in marine and terrestrial ecosystems, and sharks represent one of the most endangered groups in the ocean as a consequence of fishing exploitation, high vulnerability and a generalized lack of data on ecology and conservation status. This situation is particularly critical in the Mediterranean Sea due to its millenarian history of exploitation. Even if the white shark is a rare but persistent inhabitant of the Mediterranean Sea, its ecology in the area is still largely unknown. We have scarce information about white shark distribution and habitat use, aspects that are critical for conservation and management. The species is currently assessed as “Critically Endangered” according to the IUCN Regional Redlist criteria. In this study, we built the most comprehensive database of white shark occurrence records in the area (773 observations) and used them to characterize the spatial and temporal patterns of abundance of Mediterranean white sharks within a large temporal window (1860-2016). We fitted generalized additive models to standardized occurrence rates and used spatially disaggregated information on human coastal population abundance as a proxy of observation effort. Our results suggest a complex trajectory of population change characterized by a historical increase and a more recent steep reduction (61.5%) since the second half of 20th-century. Declines ranged between 52% and 97% across different Mediterranean sectors, with a contemporary regional contraction of the spatial distribution. For the first time, these results would inform conservation assessments, underlining the importance to produce status assessments based on population trends that are not suspected but quantitatively inferred. Furthermore, our analyses resulted instrumental to advance new hypotheses on the white shark occurrence and ecology in the Mediterranean Sea and to plan tagging programs with the purpose of collecting high-quality ecological data such distribution, population structure, foraging and habitat use.

title: Bycatch of batoids in trammel nets in the Valencian region (Spanish Mediterranean): a case of unreported and unregulated fishing
abstract_text: The biggest threats to batoids (rays and skates) in the Mediterranean are overfishing and bycatch. The protection of these species is challenging, particularly due to inadequate labeling in fishing ports or inadequate fisheries regulations. Small-scale vessels in the Mediterranean make up 83% of the total fishing fleet, being fixed nets (trammel and gill nets) the most common used gear. In the Valencia region (Spanish Mediterranean) trammel nets are the most common (51%). In this fishery batoids are an important element of bycatch, although catch data on these species is scant. The present study aims to: 1) describe the impact of bycatch (CPUE) for batoid species in trammel nets in the Valencia region, 2) address diversity, spatial and seasonal differences in batoids bycatch composition, and 3) identify and propose direct measures to asses this issue on the unreported and unregulated fishing practices in the region. From January to December 2017, both onboard observation on fishing vessels and sampling of catches at the landing site were carried out in three different ports of the Valencian region. In total, 81 sets from 14 vessels were monitored, giving a record of 429 batoid specimens of 12 different species and five families (Dasyatidae, Gymnuridae, Myliobatidae, Rajidae and Torpedinidae). The most abundant were Torpedo marmorata (25,8%; total average), Torpedo torpedo (25,4%) and Raja radula (16,3%). All the catches were discarded, sold privately or sold at market without identification at species level. There was not significant correlation between batoid’s size and the panel mesh size of trammel nets. Data collected showed seasonal differences in size and total biomass, with a higher rate of captures of larger specimens during the period from March to June. Our results highlight the need of further studies in the area and future implementation of mitigation measures, such as adequate reporting of catches.

title: Actions towards collaboration for an improved sharks bycatch management in the Mediterranean: conservation, communication and citizen science
abstract_text: The Mediterranean Sea is considered as one of the most dangerous places for sharks and rays in the world, with more than 50% of its species under risk of extinction. Fisheries bycatch is the main threat to sharks and rays in the region. Full evaluation of fisheries impact on shark populations, however, is hampered i.a. by the lack of data on post-release survival rates, highly dependent on fishing strategy and handling practices during the release of the animal, and on key nursery areas and migration routes. Proper monitoring programs are lacking in the majority of Mediterranean countries. Existing bycatch recording systems, including paper based and electronic fisheries logbooks as well as voluntary reporting tools developed by citizen science initiatives, often lack harmonization and interoperability and frequently show weak sustainability and user ownership. Furthermore, fishers and often also port authorities lack capacity to identify protected species and are not aware of legislation and procedures for landing and marketing. The SafeSharks project focuses on the Southern Adriatic adopting a comprehensive approach including 1) stakeholder engagement to raise awareness of the fishing sector on shark status and create ownership to the issue, 2) roundtables of relevant actors (scientists, seafood market and fishing sector, NGOS, authorities) to address key needs in order to improve monitoring, control and surveillance of sharks bycatch and facilitate collaboration, 3) satellite tagging to assess post release survival rates and establishment best handling and release practices and 4) seafood fraud risk assessment in the main Italian markets linked to the Southern Adriatic. Preliminary results of the project will be presented, together with the outcomes of the workshop “A Mediterranean where sharks, rays, skates, and chimeras are valued and managed for sustainability: From Citizen science to implementation of regulation for bycatch of vulnerable sharks and rays in the Mediterranean”.

title: Baseline assessment of the coastal elasmobranch fauna of eastern Cabo Verde using baited remote underwater video
abstract_text: An increasing onus on tropical elasmobranch management has revealed a paucity in data on abundance, distribution and fisheries. The Republic of Cabo Verde is drafting their national plan of action for sharks, and a lack of coastal fisheries dependent and independent information on elasmobranchs necessitates the creation of a baseline. We combined baited remote underwater video (BRUV) and interviews with traditional fishermen to create the first assessment of the diversity, distribution, and fisheries involvement of elasmobranchs around the eastern islands of Sal, Boavista and Maio, including the remote offshore reef João Valente. Over 200 hours of footage revealed 216 elasmobranchs spanning 16 species from 6 taxonomic families. Three findings were particularly notable: i) CPUE was highest in Maio, the island with the smallest human population; ii) Carcharhinidae spp. were observed in considerably greater abundance in Sal, followed by Boavista; meanwhile Maio and João Valente displayed an absence of large-bodied Carcharhinids; iii) Species richness was consistent across islands, with Boavista and Sal recorded diversity. Results from 207 fisher interviews revealed that 88% of fishers fished sharks, with endangered scalloped hammerheads cited as the most widely captured species. Most fishers (95%) noted a decline in marine resources over the past 5-10 years, with 70% perceiving significant reductions in sharks captured. Cabo Verde’s eastern islands hosts high relative diversity and abundance of coastal elasmobranchs compared to West Africa; higher trophic level species show evidence of intensive exploitation notably with increasing proximity to the capital city Praia. Results of this study are conservative: although fishers interviewed were anonymous and care was taken with the structure and delivery of survey questions, fishers were often reluctant to share information as many believe elasmobranch fisheries to be illegal. Nonetheless, our study suggests that artisanal and semi-industrial fisheries are strongly impacting coastal shark populations.

title: The fish of Turkey’s past: A recent history of disappeared species and commercial fishery extinctions for the Black and Marmara Seas
abstract_text: To document the rapidly declining abundance of Turkish marine resources, a timeline of commercial fisheries extinctions and a list of threatened or extirpated marine species are presented for the Black Sea and Sea of Marmara for Turkey. Turkish nationally reported fisheries data were compared over a 50 year period from 1967 (the first year data were spatially allocated) to 2016 to assess which species are now extirpated (i.e., currently completely absent from the reported catch data), and which species have become commercially extinct (i.e., whose catch declined by 75-99.9%). Other important taxa, with special attention paid to sharks not captured by the statistics, are discussed using accounts from peer-reviewed literature, grey-literature and personal accounts from local scientist and fishers. The Black Sea has 25 extirpated species and 19 commercially extinct marine species, while the Sea of Marmara has 22 extirpated species and 32 commercially extinct species. We interpret these extinctions and declines as indications of potential ecosystem collapses and urge management to be more effective in rebuilding the Turkish marine fisheries, before it becomes too late.

title: A blank area on the map – Molecular identification and shark population dynamics: implications for conservation based on artisanal fishing
abstract_text: Coastal ecosystems are highly affected by elevated fishing pressure, targeting a higher number of species in continental waters and being sharks and rays among the most disturbed and harvested species. The increasing demand for shark fins and meat in combination with by-catch captures has led shark populations all over the world to an alarming decline. The Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) represents an optimal opportunity to serve as a case study for shark conservation, carrying the potential for worldwide implications. However, the lack of information is still a key problem for the establishment of definitive conservation and management policies. The largest part of elasmobranch landings from artisanal fisheries are juvenile sharks; captured sharks are landed finless, decapitated, and ready to be processed. These, together with the lack of taxonomic knowledge from fisherman and fisheries control agents, make proper identification a challenging task. Therefore, the use of genetic tools for the identification of the shark species is crucial, due to the high observed abundance of juvenile sharks collected, the presence of cryptic species and important genetic population units that might probe essential for conservation and establishment of baselines for further shark research in the ETP. Here, we present barcoding and genetic diversity results from the mitochondrial NADH2 gene used for the identification of 12 species from shark landings in the Northern Colombian Pacific region (ETP) from 2016 to 2018. Two species categorized as threatened under the IUCN Red List, Sphyrna lewini (Endangered) and Carcharhinus falciformis (Vulnerable) occurred frequently in the samples analyzed (21% and 18%, respectively). Our findings are of great importance, particularly for threatened species, as the genetic diversity results showed low values compared to other species in the study. This study is the baseline for further research in the area aiming for understanding shark population dynamics, connectivity between populations as well as the identification of nursery areas.

title: Using science fuel to drive a change: a case study involving microplastics, whale sharks and stakeholders in the Maldives
abstract_text: Due to their remote location and increasing tourism, the Maldives struggle with their waste management. The environmental consequences of this are reflected in the results of a recent study reporting microplastics to be particularly abundant in this Archipelago. However, the Maldives, being a biodiversity hotspot, also feel the great responsibility to protect their unique marine habitats, home to many threatened species, including the endangered whale shark (Rhincodon typus). Whale sharks are of high economic value to this “island nation” as the opportunity to encounter them lures tourists from all over the world and tourism has become the largest economy of the Maldives. It would thus be prudent from an ecological and economic point of view to protect and preserve their habitats and achieve good environmental status. Here, we aim to open the dialogue with key stakeholders (tourism sector, policy makers, local scientists and the general public) by using findings of microplastic ingestion by whale sharks. Indeed, their feeding strategy, filtering up to 614 m3/h of sea water, make them particularly prone to microplastics ingestion. This is of concern as microplastic ingestion by other fish species has been shown to cause reductions in food uptake and predatory performance, and act as a vector of toxins, which can bioaccumulate and lead to endocrine disruption and hepatic stress. To operate at the science-society-policy interface we first engaged with stakeholders through a survey to create a shared problem framing. Second, we conducted workshops with each stakeholder individually during which we communicated our scientific findings and developed collaborative solutions to tackle the issue of plastic pollution. Future project developments will aim to empower and support stakeholders to implement their solutions, but also to contribute to their current and future efforts when introducing new regulations for marine protection.

title: Presence of Squatina oculata in Sicilian and Maltese waters
abstract_text: The Smoothback Angelshark Squatina oculata is commonly found in warm-temperate and tropical waters of the eastern Atlantic continental shelves and upper slopes, at depths ranging from 20 to 500 m, but mostly between 50 and 100 m. S. oculata is rarely distributed in the Mediterranean basin. To date this species has, in fact, been rarely encountered in Gulf of Gabes, Tunisia and, more generally, in the southern regions of the Mediterranean Sea. In 2007, four specimens were recorded from southern Italy (Strait of Sicily). The present study contributes recent data on the rare occurrence of the Smoothback Angelshark along the south-eastern Sicilian coasts through four musealized specimens and through four photographic records, besides reporting an underwater observation for Maltese waters.

title: Supporting species-specific reporting of elasmobranchs in the Falkland Islands’ fisheries
abstract_text: The waters surrounding the Falkland Islands are highly productive, supporting a diverse abundance of elasmobranchs, including ~18 species of skate. Commercial fisheries operating in these waters land 5,000-7,000 tonnes of skate each year. The fisheries consist of ‘foreign fleets’, strictly managed by the Falkland Islands Fisheries Department (FIFD). Most skate species are caught in trawl and longline fisheries. At present, all retained skate are recorded as a single multispecies assemblage, however, observer data suggests that certain species are much more commonly caught than others. Species-specific reporting (SSR) is imperative for building baseline data on individual species populations and distribution and for monitoring changes in species assemblages. SSR can also be used to help provide advice for better management and policies to ensure long-term sustainable fisheries and species diversity. Drawing on the Trust’s extensive experience creating identification (ID) materials, the FIFD and the Shark Trust began a collaborative project to develop accurate ID materials for skate to aid transition to SSR. An ID placard for the eight species of skate most commonly caught in the Patagonia Toothfish Longline Fishery was produced and translated into three languages (English, Korean, Spanish) and a framework for an ID guide was developed. The project has now expanded to include all skate species and other elasmobranchs caught as bycatch across all fleets. In addition, the skate, Dipturus chilensis (Guichenot, 1848), was recently re-described as a new species of skate (D. lamillai sp. nov.) endemic to the Falkland Islands – this has been updated on the original placard. The Shark Trust has now produced a second placard and an extended ID guide, (18 skate, one ray, six sharks) suitable for fishers, observers and the general public. This collaborative work highlights the importance of SSR as a platform for effective global fisheries management.

title: Monitoring Whale Shark populations in the Northern Red Sea using Individual Identification
abstract_text: Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) are defined by the IUCN as an endangered species, with numbers around the world quickly declining. They inhabit all tropical and warm-temperate seas, the Red Sea being the northern most part of its distribution.The Whale Shark Project, run by the NGO 'Sharks in Israel', aims to monitor the population and record all sightings of this species in an ongoing data and photo base. Up until 2019, whale shark sightings along the Israeli coast of the Aqaba bay in the Red Sea were rather rare, adding up to only a handful a year at best. However, in 2019, a record high of whale shark encounters in Israel were recorded. To date, there have been 22 observations of this species in 2019, beginning in April and continuing into early August with most sightings occurring in April (n=7) and July (n=11). Simple photo analysis reveals that all encounters were of at least four different individuals, all juveniles and sub-adults, estimated at a length of up to 5 meters. Additional analysis via Wildbook software allows for further definition of the individuals via visual mark mapping and gives the collected data a global context by unveiling information about the specific individual in different geographic locations. Monitoring the whale shark population in Israel and mapping their whereabouts can allow to establish a tailormade conservation plan, designed to protect the species on a global level.

title: Another recent record of the uncommon sharpnose sevengill shark Heptranchias perlo in the Balearic Sea (Western Mediterranean)
abstract_text: On June 26, 2019, a sharpnose sevengill shark Heptranchias perlo was captured in the Eivissa Channel by a trawler fishing boat targeting to the red shrimp Aristeus antennatus. It represents the second substantiated historical record of the species around Balearic Islands (Sub-Area GSA05 of General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean) and up to date the third one in all the Mediterranean Spanish waters. This species is cataloged as Data Deficient for the Mediterranean by the IUCN. Thus, we consider of great interest to record and spread the observations and catches that may be done on this species, in order to contribute to further assessments on its current conservation status. The specimen was captured at depth range 465-515 m at a location (average trawl coordinates) of 38°58’N 00°24’E. The specimen was an immature female of 643 mm TL. It had threadlike uteri and macroscopically recognizable but undeveloped ovaries (only with small previtelogenetic oocytes). The stomach contents was relatively abundant and contained pieces of squid arms (but no beaks) and a medium-sized piece of an unidentified teleost. Samples of muscle and liver of the shark were taken and preserved in order to be used for possible future studies. A review of the recent records of H. perlo in the Mediterranean is also presented.

title: Another piece of the evolutionary history of Atlantic skates (Chondrictyes, Rajiformes): integrating DNA barcoding approach and phylogenetic inferences
abstract_text: Conservation and long-term management plans of marine species need to be conceived upon a universally recognized key-feature: species identity. This important assignment resulted particularly arduous among skates (order Rajiformes), in which the phenotypic similarity between some taxa and the individual variability in others, entangled accurate species identification. This study confirms the power of DNA barcoding for the discrimination between skate species across the Atlantic Ocean and for its use as effective tool to minimize the risk of species misidentification and to elucidate species boundaries. In this perspective, this work compiles and establish a new fully available and well-curated barcode library, the ELASMO-ATL project, which gathered biological and molecular information of 432 skate specimens and covered coastal waters of four FAO Major Fishing Areas (27, 34, 47, 41) of the Atlantic Ocean. The evolutionary histories of 34 skate species were estimated with two concatenated mitochondrial markers (COI and NADH2) through Bayesian and species level phylogeny analyses. It was possible to discover a new evolutionary lineage within the genus Raja in the southern-most part of its distribution area and to enable deepening the relationship between South-African endemic species of Rajella. Once again, Western South African coasts and oceanographic fronts may play a fundamental role among skates’ speciation events in which the paleoclimatic and paleogeographic history joined to hydrography events could have contributed to the formation of refugial areas, characterized by geographical isolation. Subsequent contact zones in these areas between Senegal and Angola seems to constitute a continuum/cline of genetic change among some Raja species. These data successfully resolved many taxonomic ambiguities and demonstrated a highly cohesive monophyletic clustering among the order laying the foundations for further inference of evolutionary patterns suitable for addressing management and conservation issue.

title: Elasmobranch fisheries and trade in North Aegean: Six months of systematic monitoring
abstract_text: The Hellenic seas host about 67 species of elasmobranchs, 25 of which are protected, while the regulation of fishing for another 5 species is declared. The status of elasmobranch exploitation in Greece remains ambiguous, due to the fact that elasmobranch landings are recorded in aggregated categories while they are also commonly misreported; consequently accurate species-specific data are not available in a country level. Mislabeling of elasmobranch products is a common phenomenon in several markets around the globe and a recent study revealed that is a reality for Greece as well. Our work aims at monitoring the landings and the marketed products of elasmobranchs in the four major ports of the North Aegean Sea. The selected area is a hotspot for elasmobranchs as approximately 40% of their landings takes place. In this work we provide systematic data on a seasonal basis for quantifying the issue. Monthly visits in Alexandoupoli, Kavala, Michaniona (Thessaloniki) and Volos take place, collecting species-specific data in the auction markets and landing sites and flesh samples of elasmobranchs products from the fish markets for genetic identification and chemical analysis. In addition, interview based surveys are conducted to traders and consumers for better understanding the market incentives. In six months, a total of 442 species-specific records of elasmobranchs were gathered from the four auction markets and landing sites, 101 samples of elasmobranch products and 30 samples for chemical analysis. More than 30 questionnaires from traders and 100 from consumers were collected. Illegal fishing, trade and mislabelling is evident in the four sites, with some extremely threatened and protected species like Gymnura altavela (Linnaeus, 1758) being quite common. Traders, fishmongers and fishermen lack knowledge on the applied legislation as well as on the conservation status of these species, while the lack of conectivity between legislations, reinforce mislabelling and illegal trade.

title: Characteristics of whale shark Rhincodon typus around the island of St Helena, South Atlantic & the comparative impact of ecotourism
abstract_text: 328 whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) were identified using photographs and pattern recognition software between 2013 and 2017 around the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic. The highest number of whale sharks were recorded in the month of January. This is probably due to the sharks exploiting a seasonally abundant food source, such as tuna (Scombridae spp.) and other fish spawn in the waters around St Helena. Other behaviours observed included females remaining stationary in an inverted arc posture with males swimming around them, which is associated with mating behaviour in other shark species. The mean total length of the sharks was 7.63 metres, and of the sharks whose sex was determined 45.9% (133) were female, and 54.1% (157) male. Of those males, only one was juvenile as determined by clasper morphology. Worldwide, aggregations of whale sharks tend to consist of majority juvenile males. The combination of mature male and female whale sharks in the study area and the observed courtship behaviour means it is possible that the waters around St Helena are of global importance for whale shark mating. The St Helena aggregation was compared to an aggregation in the Maldives with 315 whale sharks identified over 10 years. Whale sharks in the Maldives bore a significantly higher injury rate (82.2%, p<0.001, X2 test) than those in the St Helena aggregation (9.1%), with anthropogenic injuries in Maldives at 54.9%, compared to 2.4% in St Helena. This may be a consequence of the greater number of weakly regulated ecotourism boats targeting the Maldives aggregation compared to the tightly regulated and limited ecotourism for whale sharks around St Helena.

title: Uncommon elasmobranch acquisitions in Sicilian museums
abstract_text: An important role that museums continue to play is the acquisition of new specimens with particular regard to endangered or critically endangered species. The Museo Civico di Storia Naturale di Comiso (Ragusa), founded in 1991 has more than 27,000 specimens from zoological and paleontological samples. In 2017 the Museum was recognized as a "Scientific Institution registered at the CITES Secretariat D. M. 87, 23.03.1994, IT030”. The elasmobranch collection is represented by 45 Mediterranean and 10 exotic species (14 Orders, 24 Families). A long series of international contacts with research institutes and taxidermy cabinets has allowed the acquisition of some rare specimens. Among these there are a recently acquired adult female of Chlamydoselachus anguineus Garman, 1884, of 180 cm TL, caught in 2015 in the waters of Suruga Bay, Japan Pacific Ocean and a female of Oxynotus paradoxus Frade, 1929, about 50 centimeters LT, caught in 2017 in the waters of the Gulf of Biscay, France, northeast Atlantic Ocean. Wilderness is an institution that deals with environmental studies. Founded in 1991, it has always paid particular attention to the problems of nature conservation. The company is regularly listed on the CITES list as a subject that carries out research and teaching activities. The Wilderness collection, taxidermised with the freeze-dry technique, is represented by 49 Mediterranean and 20 exotic species. It recently acquired a specimen of Mustelus fasciatus (Garman, 1913) from La Paloma, Rocha, Uruguay, a C. anguineus and a juvenile of Mitsukurina owstoni Jordan, 1898, fished in 2015 in the waters of Suruga Bay, Japan and a female of O. paradoxus, caught in 2016 in the Irish waters. All the new acquisitions were treated with modern taxidermy techniques: the two C. anguineus, M. fasciatus and M. owstoni with freeze-dry in Austria and the two O. paradoxus as dry preparations in Concarneau, France.

title: Mission (im)possible: identifying skate species accurrately, fast, easy and untrained, is that possible?
abstract_text: The identification of and distinction between some skate species is not trivial! It is already challenging to find time during busy research surveys to spend that extra time to e.g. count thorns on a huge skate and evaluate a set of additional criteria to unambigiously identify its species ID, but what about commercial fishing vessels? We conducted a set of workshops in 2019 to develop an easy ID guide for skates in Norwegian waters (~13 species) which will be tested by some commercial fishing vessels as well as some of our own research surveys until the end of 2019, followed by a feedback-based revision of this living resource. In addition, we aim to produce a wings-based ID guide for 2020 comprising the top landed skate species in Norway, which is intended as a resource for the landing sites. We will present some drafts of this wing ID for discussion. Training workshops on the use of these different resources are planned from 2020 onwards. We will present our stakeholder driven approach as well as examples of simple criteria which save time. We expect this initiative to increase the industry-participation and to ultimately yield more accurate species-specific data.

title: New grey reef shark (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos) nursery in the Mozambico channel close to Nosy be Island – Madagascar
abstract_text: Grey reef sharks (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos), are included in the IUCN red list as near threatened, however, their biology is still relatively little known. Discordant data are available on their tendency to be site fidelity, studies carried out in Australia indicate limited reef fidelity and evidence of large-scale movements within northern Australian waters, while site fidelity and residency of grey reef sharks on the outer slope of coral reefs in Palau, Micronesia, over a period of two years and nine months were detected regularly throughout another study and sharks displayed strong inter-annual residency with greater attendance at monitored sites during summer than winter months. However, it is commonly believed that Grey reef sharks display strong levels of site fidelity that persist across years, at least for some components of the population. Site fidelity is a common phenomenon in many species, including whitetip (Triaenodon obesus), tawny nurse (Ginglymostoma cirratum), blacktip (Carcharhinus melanopterus), Caribbean (C. perezi) and grey reef (C. amblyrhynchos) sharks. The degree of fidelity appears to vary according to life history stage, availability of resources and area of suitable habitat. Site fidelity is also common in adult reef sharks, although typically more sporadic when compared to juveniles, which might be partially explained by ontogenetic increases in the size of home ranges. Off Nosy be in Madagascar in the Mozambique channel, we have identified a new probable nursery that is being monitored by CSS (Centro Studi Squali) since 2017, thanks to the logistical and underwater support of the Manta Diving. Around the pinnacle of a coral reef at about 15-30 meters depth, grey reef sharks patrol daily, specimen sizes between 50cm and 200cm. The importance of identifying and reporting nursery areas for this species, is a priority to promote its proper conservation.

title: Nursery survey of Nursehound, Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758), around Monte Argentario peninsula (Tuscany, Italy) with new tools: Poseidon R.O.V. (Remote Operative Vehicule)
abstract_text: The Nursehound, Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758), is a benthonic catshark present inshore and offshore in the northeast and eastern central Atlantic, over the continental shelf between southern Scandinavia and Senegal, and is also distributed throughout the Mediterranean. This species is fished by bottom trawls, gill nets, bottom set long lines, handlines and fixed bottom nets, and occasionally by pelagic trawls. Although limited data are available on the exploitation and trends in abundance, declines have been indicated in the Mediterranean Sea, particularly around the Balearic Islands and in the northwest Mediterranean. The capacity for resilience of this species is affected by a low level of interconnectivity between isolated populations around islands far from the continental coast. Few informations are available on its biology; however, it is a large bodied species and is likely more vulnerable to population depletion than the Smallspotted Catshark (S. canicula), which also occurs in the region. Given its large size, patchy distribution and evidence of decline in the Mediterranean Sea, an assessment of at least Near Threatened is warranted (IUCN Red List. 2009). In 2018 Sharks Studies Centre activated a new project aimed at locating, around Monte Argentario Pensinsula in Tuscany (Ita), the presence of Nursehound Nursery using Poseidon R.O.V. (Remote operative vehicule), an underwater drone that can operate up to 120 meters deep with 5 hours of autonomy. The project, partially funded by the Tuscany Region (Go Green 2018), will allow to identify eggs spawning areas. The first 2 years of observations, 2018 and 2019, are presented and discussed.

title: A different way to analyze opportunistic data: the Mediterranean White Shark as a pilot study
abstract_text: Sharks represent one of the globally most endangered groups of fish, particularly in the Mediterranean Sea where 57% of the species are considered threatened by the IUCN. Occurrence sightings are increasingly scarcer in the area and targeted surveys are rare and limited to specific sectors. However new opportunities are emerging to exploit unconventional sources of data such as new methods to analyze citizen science data and other opportunistic sightings. Analyzing opportunistic records is challenging for two main reasons. First, no systematic surveys were carried out to collect these data. Hence, no information was recorded about sampling or observation effort. Second, opportunistic records are presence-only data so they need to be modeled while making inferences about possible processes generating absence and regimes of sampling effort. In this pilot study, we combined all the available data on the white shark presence in the Mediterranean Sea collecting information from different sources (MEDLEM-Mediterranean Large Elasmobranchs Monitoring and sharkPulse), and used these data to test a different approach in characterizing the spatial distribution of the species in the area from presence-only data. We used spatio-temporal Point Processes Models (PPM) both in a Maximum likelihood and Bayesian framework to analyze the Mediterranenan white shark distribution. In this way we obtained the probability of occurrence of the species in the area on a set of covariates associated to the point pattern itself (i.e. SST, fishing effort), controlling for the observation effort through the use of a simple proxy based on coastal human population trajectories. This approach can be surely extended to other species and different areas and might represent a useful tool to better characterize elasmobranchs distribution patterns and conservation status all around the world, as well as postulating new ecological hypotheses on species so far understudied for a lack of conventional scientific and adequate fisheries data.

title: The Elasmobranchs collections in the Italian Natural History Museums
abstract_text: The museums of natural history are the headquarters of the history of our Planet and are fundamental institutions, highly useful for the dissemination of scientific culture in the world. The preserved specimens have gone from simple collections of objects to teaching and scientific research tools. The museum exhibits, in addition to witnessing the presence of species in their natural environments, have become an important resource for research, necessary to understand the phylogenetic and taxonomic relationships among also the living organisms, nowadays increasingly threatened with extinction due to anthropogenic reasons. With the global biodiversity crisis, the museums of natural history have assumed the role of bank of the biodiversity definitively. The Mediterranean basin is known as one of the biodiversity ‘hot-spot’ in relation to the presence of many endemic species. However, since the Mediterranean is one of the most exploited seas on the Planet, the biodiversity is highly threatened. Regarding the study on Italian sea-life conservation, the elasmobranch collections of the museums become an important heritage favorable to improve the biological knowledges and the historical trends of this species community. For these reasons, a detailed study on the chondrichthyans collections stored in the main Italian museums was carried out. We present here a general picture of the all information gathered thanks to the collaboration among various Italian institutions.

title: Global review of elasmobranch entanglement in anthropogenic marine debris & New citizen science platform: ShaREN (Shark and Ray Entanglement Network)
abstract_text: Numerous marine taxa become entangled in anthropogenic marine debris, including cartilaginous fishes (class: Chondrichthyes, e.g. elasmobranchs [sharks, skates and rays], holocephalans [chimaeras]). Here we present research that has been conducted on the susceptibility of these taxa to entanglement in marine debris using a systematic literature review complemented by novel data collection from the social media site Twitter. We present our new online citizen science platform ShaREN (Shark and Ray Entanglement Network) to further aid data collection on the topic of elasmobranch entanglement. Our literature review yielded 47 published elasmobranch entanglement events (N = 557 animals) encompassing 34 species in all 3 major ocean basins. The most common entangling objects were ghost fishing gear (74% of animals). While investigating Twitter, we found 74 cases of elasmobranch entanglement, representing 26 species. On Twitter, ghost fishing gear was again the most common entangling material (94.9% of animals). Entanglement in marine debris is symptomatic of a degraded marine environment and is a clear animal welfare issue. We highlight a relative paucity of scientific data on this subject and collaborate with the Shark Trust UK to create ShaREN, to further data collection and enable scientists to accurately quantify elasmobranch entanglement risks and locate interaction hotspots globally.

title: Shark fishery between socio-economic and conservation issues
abstract_text: Serious concerns have been expressed by researchers about the vulnerability of shark species in the Mediterranean Sea. The state of conservation of many species is not known due to the lack of data and also the continuous bycatch, only roughly estimated, removes these organisms from their habitat indiscriminately. According to FAO, Italy is one of the biggest consumers of shark meat. The market for these products is very wide for both fresh and frozen products and the import from all over the world is also high. Cases of mislabeling about shark are frequently recorded: the major case is the sale of blue shark (Prionace glauca) as the most valuable dogfish (Mustelus spp.) the cost of which is higher than the other traded sharks. A research carried out on samples collected at the fish market of Milan, showed that 77% of the dogfish samples were found to belong to other genera of sharks. During a study conducted by us on the species authentication of seafood products, 30 samples of slice labeled as swordfish, bought in the local markets of Sicily, were processed using the consolidated method of DNA barcoding based on a relatively long fragment of 650 bp of the COI gene. A 20% of the samples were found to belong to various species of sharks in substitution of swordfish. The species of elasmobranchs detected were P. glauca, Scyliorhinus canicula, Mustelus mustelus, Isurus oxyrinchus and Oxynotus centrina. Based on the IUCN data 2016, three of the above species (??) are considered critically endangered in the Mediterranean Sea, one species is vulnerable (??). From the molecular analyses we start to collect data on these species, in particular we try to bring more details from the first part of the fish supply chain: fishermen.

title: The elasmobranch community in the central Mediterranean: change in diversity, abundance and habitat influence
abstract_text: In the marine ecosystems the cartilaginous fishes represent the oldest and most ecologically diverse vertebrates filling the upper levels of aquatic food webs with possible top-down control on the midlevel consumers. Because of their K-selected life-history (e.g. slow growth, late attainment of sexual maturity, long life spans, low fecundity) these species are particularly vulnerable to the human activities, mainly to the overexploitation, and many of them are at risk of extinction. Although sharks and skates play a key role in the biological communities, the effects of their decline on the marine ecosystem, due mostly to fishing activity, are still poorly known. Considering data coming mainly by scientific surveys (e.g. MEDITS) carried out in the last thirty years, the authors provide information on the species diversity and fluctuations of abundance of the chondrichthyes caught on the soft bottoms of the north-western Ionian Sea, focusing the analysis on the species composition change and variable vulnerability and exposure to fishing of the different species. In this respect, recent acquisitions on the distribution and abundance of elasmobranches in sensitive habitats of the Ionian and South Adriatic Sea, such as cold-water coral habitats and canyons, are reported. Since these habitats, less accessible to fishing, can provide a natural refuge for these vulnerable species, large-scale connected protected areas can be a potential management option for the cartilaginous fish conservation.

title: Why not catch the big fish? Fatty acids to support a more sustainable fishing of elasmobranchs
abstract_text: Every year in Europe thousands of elasmobranchs die for fishing and many of them are caught for commercial and human consumption. There is no shame in saying that elasmobranchs can represent a small variation to the constant consumption of bony fish. Raja clavata is one of the most common species of elasmobranchs employed along Adriatic coasts for this use. For this research, 30 specimens of Raja clavata has been collected by trawl from December 2018 till March 2019. From each specimen we obtained biometric data and then we removed fillets. The samples have been processed to obtain fatty acids profiles. Fatty acids have been extracted using Bligh e Dyer (1959) method and gaschromatography has been employed for the determination of fatty acids profiles. The rays with the larger dimensions showed a greater concentration of polyunsaturated fatty acids than smaller ones. This relationship between concentration of fatty acids and dimensions of the rays can lay the groundwork for a responsible and higher quality fishing activity. In fact, from one hand fatty acids, in particular polyunsaturated, are essential for human health. From the other hand, since these acids are more present in bigger animals (that maybe have already reproduced more than once), it appears useful the promotion of selective fishing activities towards the dimensionality of rays. Since in our country there are no limits and few regulations for the elasmobranchs fishing, these two issues could be used as useful points for the development of a more sustainable future fishing.
