title: Increasing knowledge about sharks on primary school students’: perceptions towards their vulnerability and conservation
abstract_text: For most people the word “shark” conjures images of terror and fear. As one of the greatest marine predators, sharks easily receive a reputation as killing machines; in reality, however, sharks have far more to fear from humans than humans do from sharks. Misconceptions, lack of knowledge and negative attitudes towards sharks act as barriers preventing actions required to tackle threats to shark populations, limiting the success of global shark conservation initiatives. Shark conservation would become more sustainable if public understanding of this predatory fish and an appreciation of its ecological significance could be promoted. To provide essential baseline data for planning of these educational efforts, this project investigated the perceptions of 9 to 11 years-old primary school student’s in Rende, CS, (South Italy) about sharks, and their understanding of ecological concepts and shark-related knowledge. The aim of this study was: 1- to investigate primary school students’ understanding of ecological concepts and their shark-related knowledge level and to explore their misconceptions about sharks; 2- to collect students’ perceptions or beliefs about this top predator before and after the presentation to observe if theese change; 3- to examine any correlations among students’ conceptual knowledge, perceptions and beliefs for sharks. Twelve question items were developed to assess students’ perceptions and conceptual understanding of sharks. We submitted the questionnaire to the students before and after a 30 minute long presentation about biology, behavior, relationship with human and conservation of sharks. The presentation has increased the knowledge about sharks in the primary school students. For the two specific questions about the risk of a shark attack and the danger of sharks, we found more right answers in the after-test than in the before-test. The submitted test after presentation showed more students with a new positive view on sharks. The findings indicate that these students lack sufficient knowledge and possess misconceptions about sharks and their ecological significance in the marine ecosystem.

title: Development and validation of an eDNA metabarcoding protocol to survey elasmobranch diversity
abstract_text: Assessing the presence, abundance and population status of marine elasmobranchs of high conservation concern is challenging given the harmful effects of many traditional sampling techniques and the logistical difficulty of studying these generally elusive, highly mobile and low abundance taxa. In this context, we are developing a non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding assay to improve detection of elasmobranch species from water samples, aiming at improving knowledge on them and ultimately to contribute to their conservation. The methodological workflow assesses eDNA metabarcoding efficiency in detecting species diversity, including validation of the method under controlled conditions prior to implementation in the field. For this purpose, method development and validation were carried out using water samples from the Lisbon Oceanarium, a closed system where species diversity and abundance is known, and field testing was performed in the Marine Protected Area of Arrábida, Portugal, where there is some previous knowledge on elasmobranch diversity. Several steps were performed to optimize both sampling and molecular analysis, including choosing filter pore size diameter, eDNA extraction methods and specificity and consistency of PCR amplification. Two mitochondrial gene regions were tested as molecular barcodes, namely the cytochrome oxidase subunit I (COI) and the NADH dehydrogenase subunit II (ND2), and checked for specificity to elasmobranch eDNA and taxonomic resolution. Nitrocelloluse membrane filters with 0.45 µm pore diameter performed best for water sample filtration coupled to Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit for eDNA extraction. The eDNA metabarcoding assay for ND2 proved highly specific to elasmobranch taxa and detected the species present in the main tank of Lisbon Oceanarium. Field testing showed the importance of inhibitor removal prior to PCR amplification.

title: Updating records of Squatina aculeata Cuvier, 1829 in the central and eastern Mediterranean Sea (2011-2018)
abstract_text: The three angelshark species living in the Mediterranean Sea, Squatina aculeata Cuvier, 1829, S. oculata Bonaparte, 1840 and S. squatina (Linnaeus, 1758), are listed as Critically Endangered Species for the basin. Alerted fishermen operating in the central and eastern Mediterranean waters provided information on the accidental capture of S. aculeata. Data on the captures of fifteen S. aculeata specimens collected between 2011 and 2018 from the Aegean and Libyan seas and from the waters of the Sicilian Channel and western Sicily are reported, adding information on the distribution and biology of this Critically Endangered elasmobranch species of the Mediterranean Sea. Data on sex, weight, depth of captures, fishing gears and the vessel names are given.

title: First Documented Angelshark Squatina squatina (Linnaeus, 1758) from the Saroz Bay (North Agaean Sea), Turkey
abstract_text: In this study, one female specimen of Angelshark (Squatina squatina) was incidentally caught by a commercial fisherman at a depth of 13 m on 10 May 2019 from Kabatepe Coast (North Aegean Sea, Turkey). The specimen was measured with a caliper and a precision scale in order to obtain morphometric and meristic characters including, total length, standard length, caudal length, gills opening, pre-first dorsal length, pre second dorsal length, pelvic to caudal space, eye diameter, pectoral origin, anal origin, Outer nostils, nostils between inner commers, mouth length, mouth width, first dorsal fin length, second dorsal fin length. Additionally, digestive tract and stomach content of the angelshark was examined under a loop and a stereomicroscope (Olympus, SD30 only when needed). Morphometric and meristic characters of the captured specimen are compared with the other Mediterranean records. According to our examination, upper and lower beaks of the cuttlefish (Sepia officinalis), Seranus scriba as a whole were identified. Moreover, leaves of Posidonia oceanica, Zostera marina associated with macro plastic litter (a part of plastic bag) were found in the stomach content. Detection of the macro plastic litter part in the stomach of the Angelfish is firstly recorded with this study.

title: Important Shark and Ray Areas: Mapping Critical Habitat for Sharks, Rays, and Chimaeras Globally
session_name: Theme Topic: Spatial Management as a tool for protecting elasmobranchs
abstract_text: Sharks, rays, and chimaeras (hereafter ‘sharks’) are often overlooked in spatial planning for biodiversity conservation. The Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) project, launched by the IUCN Species Survival Commission Shark Specialist Group in 2022, provides a tool to address this globally. The initiative identifies three-dimensional portions of habitat that are important for one or more shark species and have the potential to be managed for conservation. A set of science-based criteria are used to delineate these areas and consider species vulnerability, range restriction, life-history (reproduction, feeding, resting, movement, undefined aggregations), and special attributes (distinctiveness, diversity). These criteria are being applied to all environments where sharks occur across 13 ISRA regions covering the entire globe. Collaboration is paramount with experts convening at regional workshops to share information and propose important areas. Sixty five ISRAs have been delineated in the Central and South American Pacific and 75 proposals are undergoing review for the Mediterranean and Black Seas. Areas are also currently being evaluated for the Western Indian Ocean and other regions will follow. Peer-reviewed and approved ISRAs are mapped and added to a publicly available eAtlas (www.sharkrayareas.org). By centralising key information on shark habitat use and behaviour, ISRAs provide a foundation to ensure sharks are included in area-based management. This assists governments and policymakers in meeting global biodiversity and conservation targets, especially when such areas are overlapped with other approaches such as Important Marine Mammal Areas (IMMAs). Results from the ISRA initiative will support shark conservation by increasing information available when considering spatial management of these highly threatened species.
keywords: Important Shark and Ray Areas; Mediterranean Sea; Spatial planning; Area-based management; Shark conservation

title: Functional role of Gabon's coastal waters for two shark species, Sphyrna lewini (Griffith & Smith, 1834) and Carcharhinus limbatus (Müller & Henle, 1839)
session_name: Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
abstract_text: Large sharks are important predators in marine ecosystems, influencing the overall functioning of ecosystems and the trophic connectivity between different regions (Heithaus et al., 2008; Estes et al., 2011). However, they face intense fishing pressure, particularly in coastal areas that serve as nurseries for many juvenile sharks (Fowler et al., 2005; Heupel et al., 2007). Understanding the spatial and temporal ecology of sharks in interaction with fisheries, especially in coastal ecosystems such as estuaries and lagoons, is crucial for their conservation. Many shark species, including Sphyrna lewini (scalloped hammerhead shark) and Carcharhinus limbatus (blacktip shark), are considered threatened with extinction (Dulvy et al., 2014). Recent observations in artisanal fishing in Gabon have revealed an abundance of juvenile sharks belonging to these two species, suggesting the presence of undocumented nurseries. The southern coast of Gabon, with its lagoon complexes and mangrove habitats, could play a key role in maintaining shark populations in the equatorial Atlantic (Cadenat et al., 1955; Mourier et al., 2013). This study aims to demonstrate the existence of nurseries for Sphyrna lewini and Carcharhinus limbatus in Gabon by studying captures, the maturity of captured individuals, and their trophic ecology.
keywords: shark; fisheries; nursery; ecology; conservation

title: Sensitivity analysis and spatial distribution of elasmobranchs in Irish waters
session_name: Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
abstract_text: Over one third of elasmobranch species are threatened with extinction with nearly all species impacted by fisheries, typically from bycatch. While much research has been conducted on the impacts of certain threats on elasmobranchs, i.e., fishing, climate, discarding, and finning, there is a gap in the knowledge of how elasmobranch distributions might respond to population decline as a result of these threats. Furthermore, not all species will recover at the same rate, as some species are intrinsically more sensitive than others. Our goal was to determine the sensitivity of local elasmobranch species and highlight areas where these species and threats consistently overlap. Here we have determined the biological sensitivity of 44 species of elasmobranch found in Irish waters using the metric rmax, the maximum intrinsic rate of population increase. Oviparous species were found to have higher rmax than than ovoviviparous species in general, and the deep sea species had the lowest rmax, determining these species to be the most sensitive. Next we applied a species distribution modelling (SDM) approach to predict the distribution of 3 sensitive elasmobranch species found in Irish waters, as determined by rmax. Projections identified a change in the spatial distribution and extent of several species, with the results used to identify potential ‘hotspots’ of sensitive elasmobranchs in Irish waters based on intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Outputs of this work will help to improve the understanding of the local variability of elasmobranch species and provide support to expand and improve the management of protected areas and species.
keywords: Sensitivity; Species distribution models; rmax; Elasmobranchs; Fisheries

title: The distribution of juvenile stages and eggcases of skates (Rajidae) around the British Isles
session_name: Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
abstract_text: Skates (Rajidae) are important commercial species around the British Isles, yet there is currently limited information to aid the identification of potentially important habitats, such as spawning and nursery grounds. The neonates and juveniles of skate species have been recorded in scientific trawl surveys, with juveniles of most species proportionally more frequent in beam trawl surveys than in otter trawl surveys. The Great Eggcase Hunt is a long-standing (2003 to present) citizen science recording project that collates georeferenced data for elasmobranch eggcases, primarily from around the British Isles. This provided verified species-specific data for a total of 227,407 specimens from 11 skate species. Purse Search Ireland provided a further 2,491 records of 10 skate species. Eggcases from the genus Raja were the most frequently observed skate eggcases from much of the British coastline, and juveniles were captured in inshore waters of England and Wales. The juveniles of Raja microocellata were most common in shallow water, and the limited data available for R. undulata also indicates that any nursery grounds for this species would also be in shallow water. Juveniles of the genus Leucoraja occurred further offshore, although only the eggcases of L. naevus were recorded regularly on trawl surveys (with an L. fullonica eggcase recorded just once). The earliest free-living stages also occurred offshore. An improved knowledge of spawning and nursery grounds can be used to aid fisheries management and marine spatial planning, and may also inform the emerging interest in Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs).
keywords: citizen science; essential fish habitat; northeast Atlantic; Rajiformes; trawl surveys

title: First evidence of dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) gestation in eastern Mediterranean Sea
session_name: Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
abstract_text: All elasmobranchs are fully protected from fishing practices in Israel. In this ‘safe haven’, research led by the Morris Kahn Marine Research Station’s Marine Apex Predator Laboratory has shown that dusky sharks (Carcharhinus obscurus) and sandbar sharks (C. plumbeus) return to aggregate in the winter months (November-May) along the Israeli coastline (1-20 m depth; est. 80-100 individuals). We expect that they inhabit these areas due to the warm water discharge relative to the ambient winter temperatures (22-25°C from the power plant; ambient 16-18°C). Ours is the only long-term catch-and-release programme in the Mediterranean Basin. Currently, both species belong to Annex III of the Barcelona Convention and are evaluated as ‘Data Deficient and ‘Endangered’ on the IUCN Mediterranean Red List, respectively. Female sandbar sharks are increasingly observed with each tagging season in Israel and since 2018, we have proof that the dusky sharks are inhabiting this space during some stage of their gestation, yet we still do not know where their parturition grounds are. To answer this, we collaborated with Dr James Sulikowski, leading expert of shark reproductive biology, and co-developer of the innovative Birth-Alert Tag with Lotek Wireless. With funding from National Geographic, this state-of-the-art intrauterine satellite tag was deployed in one gravid dusky shark in April 2023 after confirmation of pregnancy via ultrasonogram, with further samples taken for physiological analyses. Further detections of this shark via acoustic transmitter were made until late May, which is unusual for this species. We present this suite of information relating to non-invasive methods.
keywords: eastern Mediterranean Sea; dusky shark; reproductive physiology; intrauterine tag; habitat usage

title: Diel vertical migrations of the blonde skate (Raja brachyura) and the spotted skate (R. montagui) in the Northeast Atlantic
session_name: Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
abstract_text: Horizontal and vertical movements of marine organisms are reflective of habitat preference and behavioural patterns in activity. Since the development of electronic monitoring devices, studies into the migrations and movements of many marine species are increasing. However, such studies into the vertical movements of benthic predators remain understudied. In this study, blonde skates, Raja brachyura, and spotted skates, R. montagui, were tagged with ‘pop-off’ data storage tags in the North Sea and English Channel. Diel vertical migrations, time-at-depth profiles and activity budgets were used to determine space-use patterns and preferences concerned with depth and temperature for mature individuals. The outcomes of this research will contribute a deeper understanding of the underlying processes that drive fish movements and distribution

title: Rapid transboundary movements of vulnerable porbeagle sharks support need for continued cooperative research and management approaches
session_name: Session 1: Insights into the spatial ecology of elasmobranch fish
abstract_text: Distribution of species across regulatory and physical boundaries poses a recognised challenge to effective management and research, and these transboundary species tend to suffer more-severe population declines. Large pelagic sharks like the porbeagle, Lamna nasus, are particularly vulnerable due to their life history characteristics including their highly migratory behaviour, whereby the latter is particularly challenging for management in European waters where management jurisdictions change over small spatial scales. We used high-resolution satellite tags to demonstrate that individual porbeagles in the region display high inter-individual variation in behaviour, undertaking very rapid movements (up to 100 km per day) through multiple EEZs and physical habitats, transiting different management zones in a matter of days along different paths. These data highlight the value of existing and the urgent need for continued regional collaboration and cross-border funding mechanisms to maximise research impact to fill knowledge gaps and improve conservation outcomes for vulnerable and highly mobile shark species.
keywords: Lamna nasus; telemetry; biologging; management; conservation

title: A non-invasive approach to estimate reproductive timing of elasmobranchs using photographs and citizen science
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: Identifying the timing of key life history events, such as mating, is important for conserving endangered species. Yet, for many elasmobranchs, there is a paucity of data on reproductive timings. Developing low-cost and non-invasive methods for estimating elasmobranch reproductive timings could assist in closing the knowledge gap and aid collecting reproductive information on more species. The flapper skate (Dipturus intermedius) is a critically endangered elasmobranch and the largest skate found in European waters. A large flapper skate photo-ID database exists, featuring photographs taken throughout the year provided by members of the public. Here, we present novel work making opportunistic use of the flapper skate photo-ID database to estimate flapper skate reproductive timing. A methodology was developed to identify the occurrence of three indicators of reproductive activity visible in photographs: pelvic swelling, bite wounds, and scratch wounds. Over 2000 images were examined for presence of each indicator and the seasonality of their occurrence was analysed via generalised additive models. Results suggest flapper skate mate over winter and lay eggs in winter and spring. The findings are corroborated by existing literature, supporting the approach as a valid method for estimating elasmobranch reproductive timing. The developed approach for analysing images could be applied to other species and make use of citizen science, providing another route for understanding reproduction in elusive elasmobranchs.
keywords: flapper skate; reproductive cycle; citizen science; photo ID; rajidae

title: Mining social media for vital Elasmobranch information in data poor regions and conflict zones: The Gaza strip as a case study
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: A huge gap in environmental information exists in conflict regions where access to scientists ranges from unsafe to impossible. Previously unknown knowledge of Elasmobranchii presence, composition, and distribution can provide valuable fisheries information regarding the exploitation of elasmobranch species and for creating comprehensive conservation strategies. However, the diversity, ecology, behavior, and many other characteristics of these species in conflict zones remain virtually unknown, which is a major cause for concern. Traditional species assessments rely on in-situ observations, market surveys, and regulatory authorities forcing fisheries to self-report their catch. Conflict areas present a unique challenge, lacking formal regulation or scientific access. Here, we report the first use of social media monitoring for the extent of the Elasmobranch fishery in the Gaza Strip (east Mediterranean), a conflict region previously lacking any information. Our database consists of 3 years of daily reported catch from 16 fish stores and social media fishery-related influencers in the Gaza Strip. We collected 1530 data points belonging to 4619 individuals of 20 species. The analysis of the data sheds light on previously unknown temporal, spatial, and seasonal trends in elasmobranch catch distribution and relations to changes in the access to maritime areas due to local conflict escalations. We demonstrate this approach as a relatively accurate and inexpensive data mining procedure, allowing the quantification and normalization of multiple observations of caught and targeted fish into a uniformed geo-spatial-temporal system- making it a prime candidate for future endeavors in other data-poor regions and conflict zones in coastal areas.

title: Enabling a wider range of people to engage with marine conservation using elasmobranchs in Wales
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: The environment sector, including organisations working to protect the marine environment, is the second-least diverse in the UK. There is an urgent need to address barriers to participation and diversify opportunities for involvement in conservation and research, as the marine environment has a vital role in natural, cultural, social and economic heritage for all communities. Project SIARC (Sharks Inspiring Action and Research with Communities) uses flagship elasmobranchs in Wales (angelshark, blue skate, common stingray, flapper skate, spurdog, and tope) to bring together local communities, fishers, researchers and government to cultivate a new appreciation and open-up access to the underwater environment in Wales. A major part of our work is to identify approaches that enable a wider range of people to engage with marine conservation in Wales and tackle the lack of diversity and inclusion within Project SIARC, thereby contributing to wider systemic change. We are on the start of our journey and to-date have focused on Project SIARC’s community initiatives in North Wales. Meetings, interviews and discussions with local communities allowed us to listen and learn from personal experiences, gathering information to produce a draft ‘Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Strategy’. This presentation will share the approach we have taken to date and some of the key learnings Project SIARC is a collaboration led by the Zoological Society of London and Natural Resources Wales, with six partners and several collaborators. It is made possible thanks to Welsh Government’s Nature Networks Fund, National Lottery Heritage Fund and On the EDGE Conservation.

title: First toxicological study in two commercial shark species from a Mediterranean Marine Protected Area
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: Large urban and industrial settlements, and the intense maritime traffic make the Mediterranean one of the most polluted areas in the world. This basin hosts considerable marine biodiversity, including many elasmobranchs, which are extremely vulnerable to environmental contamination due their life history traits. The impact of this threat on the cartilaginous fishes is still poorly studied, as well as the possible consequences for human health, in case of consumption of sharks, are uncertain. To fill this knowledge gap, quantitative and qualitative assessments of three groups of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) were carried out in the muscle and liver of two shark species, Mustelus punctulatus and Mustelus mustelus, caught in the Marine Protected Area (MPA) of Egadi Islands (South-Central Mediterranean Sea) between 2021 and 2023. As sharks are one of the top predators inhabiting the MPA, they can be considered a bioindicator of the local environmental status. Paradoxically, although M. punctulatus and M. mustelus have considerable commercial value for human consumption in the MPA, they are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN in the Mediterranean. Regarding POPs levels, the results showed a trend of PCBs > DDTs >> HCB in liver and muscle for both species. Our results can significantly contribute to clarify the toxicological status of these species, allowing a first evaluation of the real risks both for the local marine life and for human health.

title: Citizen science in the Mediterranean Sea reveals aspects of the ecology of the nursehound shark, Scyliorhinus stellaris
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: Very little is known about the biology and ecology of the nursehound shark Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758), a medium-sized catshark in severe decline in the Mediterranean Sea, assessed as Near Threatened (Vulnerable in the Atlantic) by the IUCN. Here we present results emerging from the first 10 years of the Stellaris project (2013-2023), an underwater field monitoring project in the largest egg-case nursery area known in Italian waters, the Santa Croce Bank (Gulf of Naples, Central Tyrrhenian Sea). This ongoing citizen science project provides insights on basic reproductive information on this species in the wild, such as: seasonality, development, predation and natural mortality rates, and indications that this nursery area is in decline. Photo-identification reveals that this area is also a resting area for adults of both sexes, which is used year-round and over multiple years. This nursery area is a no-fishing zone and falls within a Natura 2000 site. In spite of its protected status, illegal fishing occurs as the whole Gulf is subject to intense artisanal and recreational fishing pressure. Results of the Stellaris project allowed the Santa Croce Bank to be identified by the IUCN as an ISRA, an Important Shark and Ray Area, highlighting the importance of this refuge and the need for increased management and conservation actions for this neglected species. These results also highlight the value of citizen science in making tangible conservation contribution.
keywords: nursehound; citizen science; reproduction; photo-identfiication

title: New findings on the understudied population of sharks and rays in the Red Sea from data collected through social media
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: Sharks and rays in the Red Sea region are under intense fishing pressure, heavy development, and extensive tourism load. The IUCN report on the status of sharks and rays in the Arabian Sea and adjacent waters from 2017 found that at least half of the species are endangered. Based on these species assessments, in the Red Sea alone the number of endangered species is alarmingly higher, presenting a state of danger to almost all cartilaginous fish species that live in it. Research, conservation, and enforcement are scarce in the region. We have established a citizen science project SRS (sharks and rays in the Red Sea), based on the MECO Protocol, collecting observations from the public through social networks with the aim of gathering up-to-date basic biological and ecological information. Over 2,500 observations have been collected to date, mostly from the Gulf of Aqaba. Observations include 18 species of batoids and 14 species of sharks (82% and 18%, respectively). Our collected data has added new species records to the Gulf of Aqaba region and revealed information about their seasonality, reproduction, and distribution. These data provide essential ecological information in a region that is largely understudied and is crucial for planning conservation and management in the future.
keywords: Red Sea; Citizen science; Social Media; Sharks and Rays; Distribution pattern

title: The value of scientific data, citizen science, and collaboration with stakeholders in developing a Recovery Plan
session_name: Session 2: Citizen science I: The utility of social media and Local Ecological Knowledge
abstract_text: Angelsharks, Squatina squatina, can be seen relatively frequently by divers and fishers in the Canary Islands, a unique stronghold for the species. Due to their benthic ecology and coastal location, angelsharks are particularly susceptible to accidental capture in fisheries and habitat degradation. As a result of this, angelsharks are now listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. In 2019, angelsharks were listed under the Spanish Endangered Species List for Canary Island waters as "In danger of extinction", the highest level of protection within this legislation. Following this listing, the development of a Recovery Plan was mandated, which sets out suitable measures for the management and conservation of angelsharks. Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI) conducted a comprehensive series of in-person and online surveys to compile crucial information regarding angelshark interactions, perceptions, and potential protective measures, involving three primary interaction groups: divers, recreational fishers, and commercial fishers. This information, combined with ASP:CI scientific research, was augmented by a collaborative workshop, which engaged stakeholders representing various interests. Together, these efforts facilitated the identification of conservation areas and the co-designing of specific measures to ensure the future preservation of Angelsharks within their expansive stronghold. This presentation will delineate the key findings derived from this work, emphasizing the importance of employing a participatory approach in designing conservation strategies for this Critically Endangered species. This work, led by ASP:CI, was funded by Shark Conservation Fund and through a contract with the Canary Islands Government, co-financed by the FEDER 2014-2020 Operational Program.
keywords: Angelshark; Canary Islands; Recovery Plan; Critical Areas; Conservation Measures

title: The History and Current Management of the NE Atlantic Spurdog Fishery
abstract_text: Spurdog (Squalus acanthias), otherwise known as Spiny or Picked Dogfish, are members of the dogfish (Squalidae) family. They are distinguished by the presence of a spine in front of each dorsal fin. They have a wide distribution, mainly inhabiting temperate waters. This species was originally listed on the IUCN Red List as Critically Endangered, but through a non-genuine change in 2015, Spurdog was changed to Endangered in Europe (IUCN, 2015). In the Northeast Atlantic, there has been a fishery for Spurdog since the early 20th century. This population was overexploited which led to population decline. Various management measures have been put in place to aid recovery of this population, including placing Spurdog on the Prohibited species list. In 2022, ICES gave advice that the population could support a fishery for 2023 and 2024. In 2023, the fishery was reopened with a TAC of 17,353 tonnes (t) across the region. The UK has a quota of 4,825 t in Western waters and 2,781 t in the North Sea. As of October 2023, 194.0 t (4.0%) and 95.0 t (4.6%) of these quotas have been landed respectively. This presentation discusses the management history of Spurdog and the possible dangers of reopening a fishery on tentative signs of recovery.
keywords: Spurdog; Fisheries; Management

title: Unraveling the population structure of Northeast Atlantic spurdog (Squalus acanthias) stock: insights from mitochondrial DNA to genome-wide data
abstract_text: The spurdog (Squalus acanthias Linnaeus, 1758) Northeast Atlantic stock is managed as a single unit and has undergone a long period of overfishing, especially in the 1950s/1960s, which has caused its population to collapse. There are now signs of population growth but it remains listed as “Endangered” and overexploitation may have had an impact on its genetic composition. Limited data are available on the stocks genetic structure and properly delineating a stock unit for fisheries management is crucial to allow sustainability of the exploited population. Population genetics provides valuable insights into connectivity and genetic distinctions among individuals from different areas. Looking at genetic diversity within and between populations is also important in terms of population resilience in the face of climate change or other pressures such as overexploitation. A first assessment of the population structure was done using the NADH dehydrogenase subunit 2 (ND2) mitochondrial marker sequenced from 48 spurdogs sampled along the Norwegian part of the Northeast Atlantic. 25 unique haplotypes were distinguished, showing high genetic diversity in Norwegian waters, but no genetic distinction between sampling locations. To provide more accurate population level data, over 89 individuals from identical locations were used for genome-wide analysis, involving 53492 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) derived from Restriction-site associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq). Clustering analysis revealed subpopulations along Norwegian waters. This study presents this population structure and discusses their relevance for regional fishery management purposes.
keywords: Population genomics; Spurdog; Conservation genetics

title: Do sharks shiver when it gets warmer?
abstract_text: In the ocean, mobile species exhibit diverse movements across different spatial and temporal scales. Understanding the drivers behind these movements is essential for effective management and predicting responses to a changing ocean environment. A multitude of environmental cues, such as temperature and salinity, have been shown to affect the movements of elasmobranch species. However, it is increasingly recognized that social drivers may also influence movement. We conducted an acoustic telemetry study in a partially enclosed sea loch on the west coast of Scotland to investigate the movements and habitat selection of spurdog (Squalus acanthias). Spurdog segregate based on size and sex, and these subgroups display a high range of movements, from transatlantic movements to coastal residency. Some subgroups also display high levels of relatedness, suggesting kinship bonds within subgroups. Our findings revealed that spurdog exhibited a high level of year-round residency within the loch and that temperature plays a pivotal role in their habitat selection. Additionally, subgroups within the population display different habitat choices, which may be caused by underlying population social processes. This study underscores the importance of understanding all drivers of animal movement. Identifying sites that promote residential behaviour can aid in developing effective management strategies for species, like the spurdog. However, it is equally crucial to comprehend the social drivers of movement, as they can significantly influence habitat choices. By considering the interplay between environmental and social factors, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of animal movements and enhance conservation efforts for these mobile ocean species.
keywords: residency; Movement drivers; spurdog; Squalus acanthias; acoustic telemetry

title: Spiny dogfish behaviour in Norwegian fjords
abstract_text: Spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) is an Endangered top predator with an antitropical distribution, including extensive use of the fjords in southern and western Norway. Increasingly, these fjords are subjected to warming surface water temperatures and hypoxic bottom water. Habitat compression of spiny dogfish is predicted to instigate increased conflict between the sharks and the fisheries and aquaculture industries. To investigate if varying oxygen levels affect their depth use, we tagged more than 80 spiny dogfish with acoustic transmitters instrumented with depth, acceleration, and temperature sensors to reveal any spatiotemporal depth patterns. Furthermore, spiny dogfish swim in groups based on sex and/or size, thus a social network analysis was performed to check whether the tagged individuals exhibited interactions across time or space. Preliminary results indicate that the spiny dogfish utilize an extensive part of the water column, and most tagged individuals interact with several other spiny dogfish.
keywords: Squalus acanthias; Deoxygenation; Acoustic telemetry; Social network analysis; Behaviour

title: Use of space from the population to the individual level of commercial relevant shark species (Mustelus spp. and Squalus acanthias) in the Northern Adriatic Sea using a multidisciplinary approach
abstract_text: In the Northern Adriatic Sea (FAO-GSA 17), fishery exploitation of marine resources influenced communities and the ecosystem (Sguotti et al., 2022). In the last decades, elasmobranch species, characterized by slow growth rate and low fecundity, have been depleted due to fishing activities (Barausse et al., 2014; Ferretti et al., 2013). Despite being landed as by-catch or seasonal target catch, first evidence of population increase in abundance is highlighted for the smooth hounds (Mustelus spp.), while the spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) continues to decline (Maioli et al., 2023). Since several approaches suggested the occurrence of seasonal movements of these species (Manfredi et al., 2010; Bonanomi et al., 2018; Barbato et al., 2021), this study aims at identifying: (i) seasonal use of space of these species using fishery-dependent data from bottom otter trawls (OTB) collected within the European Data Collection Framework; (ii) spatial hotspots of observed landing per unit effort (LPUE) from coupled VMS and logbook OTB data; (iii) preliminary movement ecology aspects using conventional tagging (2017-2023) and acoustic telemetry (2022-2023) at individual-level. The first objectives allowed to identify a different seasonal use of space between the smooth hounds and the spiny dogfish, seasonal hotspot of LPUE and refined identification of areas where young-of-the-year, juveniles and adults occur. In addition, preliminary results of movement ecology highlighted site fidelity, residency and transboundary movement at individual level. Given the lack of management measures for such species, the combination of these approaches can provide essential information to set effective spatial management measures for these species.
keywords: spatial management; fishery; Triakidae; Squalidae; Use of space

title: Spurdog all the way
abstract_text: Mobile sharks are more at risk of encountering human activities such as fisheries, putting high bycatch pressure on shark populations. Spurdog (Squalus acanthias) was historically exploited by a well-documented fishery, however, relatively little is known about their large-scale movements, habitat preferences, and population dynamics after the stock collapse in the late 1990s. Over the past years, we used a variety of data types and methods, like trawl and longline surveys, fishery bycatch and environmental data, dissections, satellite tagging and spatial mapping, to decipher the spatial distribution, movement patterns, diet and life history composition of spurdog in Norwegian and northern Northeast Atlantic (NEA) waters. We found that they prefer relatively warm and shallow waters (<150 m) and stay close within coastal waters while exhibiting diel vertical migrations. The latter could imply them following their prey, which we identified as mainly bony fishes based on >500 analysed stomachs. Based on overall 5,000 dissected individuals mainly from fisheries bycatch, we found that the recruitment may have increased considerably faster in the recent two decades than previously projected, which resulted in a gradually younger population of gravid females (50% maturity at 9.3 years). This faster population recovery is reflected in the new assessment of the NEA spurdog stock by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea. The resulting fishing quota for the first time since 2009, makes close monitoring and efforts to increase our understanding of its dynamics, population structure, and responses to changing environmental conditions even more important.

title: Bridging the gaps that hidder elasmobranch conservation: Key findings of a CITES and ICCAT-focused policy analysis
abstract_text: The success of international conservation agreements relies on proper implementation at the national level. Because elasmobranchs are considered both commodities and wildlife, governments’ approaches to associated fisheries and environment treaty obligations are often misaligned. Scrutiny of this performance is lacking and represents a core yet surmountable challenge to effective policies and ultimate population rebuilding. The Shark League (a coalition including Shark Trust, Ecology Action Centre, and Shark Advocates International) will soon release a gap analysis that examines the effects of Atlantic shark and ray protection measures under various treaties, primarily the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and the International Commission for Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT). Based on an evaluation of the performance of ICCAT Parties and Cooperators with respect to various obligations for CITES-listed elasmobranchs, we highlight key gaps between concrete restrictions and conservation needs. Recommendations for priority improvements at national and international levels extend beyond government action to include specific suggestions for elasmobranch conservationists and interested scientists. Aims focus on better integration of fisheries and environmental agency activities to fulfill elasmobranch policy commitments across treaties, but also include improved fisheries and trade information, more rigorous conservation standards, and expanded assistance, as well as new safeguards for under-protected species. Because overfishing is the primary driver of shark and ray depletion, bridging these divides is critical to securing a brighter outlook for elasmobranchs in the Atlantic and beyond.
keywords: fisheries; trade; policy; CITES; ICCAT

title: What the EU’s Marine Strategy Framework Directive did and did not change for sharks and rays
abstract_text: The evaluation of policy effectiveness and impact is a crucial step in the policy cycle, to see if the agreed targets are met and to give guidance for improving future policies and legislation. One of the fundamental European Union (EU) Directives for Nature Conservation, the Habitats Directive, did not include conservation of elasmobranchs at the time it was drafted in 1992 and has not been updated to address this gap in the 30 years since. This means that elasmobranchs do not feature in Nature2000, which forms the basis for protected areas. However, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) from 2008, opened a window of opportunity for elasmobranch- related measures both in spatial protection and fisheries management, but has it delivered? Here, we assessed EU Member States’ (EU MS) efforts to integrate elasmobranchs in their national monitoring and programmes of measures under the MSFD, and if these filled in the gaps between EU policies. Results are mixed: whilst some EU MS, such as the Netherlands and Italy, report shark-specific measures under the MSFD, others generally refer to existing obligations in relation to monitoring and conservation under EU, international, and regional legal frameworks. There are no Marine Protected Areas set up under the MSFD that aim to protect elasmobranchs specifically in any EU MS. Based on the review of EU MS reporting under the MSFD, we provide advice on furthering shark conservation at EU level and how this relates to contemporary legal and policy developments in the EU and at international level.
keywords: Marine policy; Implementation; Shark conservation; European Union; Fisheries management

title: Synthesis of ten years of illegal trade of Elasmobranch products in the French online market
abstract_text: The illegal wildlife trade is recognized to be the fourth most lucrative transnational crime after drugs, arms and human trafficking. Marine species are subject to a vast range of commercial exchange despite their listing under Washington Convention (CITES). DRDH started an online survey about products of elasmobranch sold on Internet. The study primarily focused on sawfish rostrum which represented more than 3000 cases. In 2021, the work was extended to shark jaws and heads, but also reptiles such as marine turtles, crocodiles or protected marine mammals. A synthesis of 10 years of follow up was produced giving elements on the estimation of amount of money the diversity of species and geographic origins of the different pieces. The results the juridical victories are discussed in the context of global urgency for marine biodiversity worldwide.
keywords: Illegal Trade; Sawfish; Juridic; Marine species; CITES

title: The Netherlands Shark and Ray Action Plan: a case study in international cooperation
abstract_text: The Netherlands Shark and Ray Action Plan (SARAP) dates from 2017. It was reviewed in 2021 and there is currently a new action plan which will run until 2027. The objectives of the SARAP fall under Descriptor 1 of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) ‘Biodiversity’ and aim to improve the population size, distribution and condition of sharks and rays in Dutch waters. Nine of the 15 actions in the plan address European Regulations, Frameworks and Directives, as well as international conventions. All require international cooperation. These actions are not new and have been on the European agenda for a number of years. Since 2017 the EU STECF (Scientific, Technical, Economic Commission for Fisheries) has initiated three expert working groups specifically on elasmobranchs, covering skate and ray management, the implementation of the EU regulation on finning and assessment of the impact of the 2009 European Community Shark Action Plan. These meetings resulted in recommendations to advance the management and conservation of the species. Concurrently, the ICES Working Group Elasmobranch Fishes provides the science to improve stock assessments and to advise on fishing opportunities. In the past years new species have been listed on CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna) and CMS (Convention on Migratory Species), leading to obligations from the contracting parties. Although some progress is being made, real change has yet to take place. This paper will present the Netherlands Shark and Ray Action Plan as a case study in international cooperation.
keywords: Action Plan; international cooperation; management; conservation; EU legislation

title: Stakeholders' perception of sharks and rays: is there space for conservation?
abstract_text: Effective conservation measures are urgently needed for elasmobranchs. People possess significant power in driving conservation efforts, but elasmobranchs, known for historically evoking irrational attitudes, have been overlooked. Educational events improving peoples’ perception might aid conservation action. Fishery management measures are also necessary, but fishers’ willingness to adopt them must be assessed. To investigate propensity for conservation, the LIFE ELIFE project (Elasmobranchs Low-Impact Fishing Experience LIFE18 NAT/IT/000846) aims at evaluating stakeholders’ attitude and the impact of educational events using questionnaires/interviews. Participating to educational events improved people’s attitude towards elasmobranchs. Respondents indicating fear and danger as the main feelings decreased from 22.0% and 29.8% in the group not experiencing educational events (N=542) to 11.2% and 14.6% in the group that experienced them (N=121). Moreover, the percentage of respondents thinking that elasmobranchs are endangered (76.8% versus 84.8%), that more species should be protected (77.3% versus 88.9%), and of those willing to change their behaviours to aid elasmobranchs’ conservation (92.9% versus 100%) increased. Regarding fishers (N=136), only 16.0% reported a perception of decrease in elasmobranch abundances; however, fishers stated that their category should contribute to elasmobranchs’ conservation (70.4%) and that some species should be protected (50.7%). Despite 56.3% of fishers were not aware of potential fishery management measures (i.e., gear modifications), when informed, 60.9% declared they would adopt them. These preliminary results are promising; people’s positive attitude can be used to urge decision makers to adopt concrete conservation initiatives, which are likely to be more easily accepted by fishers given their willingness to collaborate.
keywords: conservation; social science; stakeholder; fishers; general public

title: A gap analysis on shark and ray research and conservation in the Caribbean
abstract_text: We present the results of a Gap analysis carried out in the summer of 2023 on the elasmobranchs of the Southeastern Caribbean. The geographical scope of this project concerns the whole of the Lesser Antilles, as well as the Dominican Republic, Haiti and Jamaica to the west, and the exclusive economic zones of the countries and territories of the Guiana plateau to the southeast. As most of this area encompasses the waters of Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and other small autonomous nations the marine life in general has not been extensively studied. Our approach was threefold, firstly we focussed on establishing an overview of the species present in the area and the research effort that had gone in to them, secondly we made an overview of the research conducted in the waters of all countries in our area of interest and lastly we made an overview of existing conservation and management measures and the level to which these were implemented. We based our findings on information gathered through a literature review as well as from interviews with regional and local experts. The research is part of the CAMAC project, for CAribbean marine Megafauna and anthropogenic Activities led by the SPAW Regional Activities Centre. The CAMAC project works to improve knowledge Caribbean mega fauna (mammals, sharks & rays and turtles) and strengthen regional collaboration. The aim is to provide recommendations and tools to reduce the negative impacts of interactions between marine megafauna and human activities.
keywords: review; Caribbean; gap analysis; SIDS

title: Where is the Spiny butterfly ray, Gymnura altavela?: aggregative behaviour in the shallow coastal zones
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: The presence of spiny butterfly rays, Gymnura altavela, in waters less than 20 m deep off the Canary Islands shows marked seasonality, with relatively high abundances in the summer and autumn. Large aggregations of sometimes hundreds of individuals, primarily females, appear in specific shallow areas of the archipelago and seem to be associated with the seasonal variation in water temperature. This seasonal pattern of presence or absence in shallow areas suggests that spiny butterfly rays migrate into deeper waters or other unknown areas during the rest of the year. G. altavela shows sexual dimorphism; in our study, females were larger and more abundant than males, with a sex ratio of 1:18.9. The species’ estimated asymptotic length, L∞, was 183.75 cm and thus close to the common length reported for the species (200 cm). The von Bertalanffy growth constant (k) oscillated between 0.210 and 0.310 year−1, as similarly described for the species in the Western North Atlantic off the U.S. coast. From June to November, the seawater temperature oscillated between 19 and 24 ◦C, and massive aggregations of females occurred at 22–24 ◦C and in a few specific sandy beaches on the islands. Spiny butterfly rays, mostly females, show a preference for aggregating in shallow waters during summertime, probably conditionate to mating or breeding behaviour.
keywords: Behaviour; biodiversity; conservation; movement

title: First insights into the last known population of guitarfishes in the Western Mediterranean. A critical area for these and other endangered species of batoids in Spain?
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: The Cabo de Palos-Islas Hormigas marine reserve in Southeast Spain stands as an outstanding conservation model, boasting one of the highest fish biomasses among Mediterranean Marine Protected Areas (MPAs). However, just beyond its boundaries, populations of highly threatened elasmobranchs appear to critically rely on this area unnoticed and unprotected. Since March 2023, over a hundred photographs from divers, snorkelers, and fishers have been collected and analysed, revealing the area´s potential significance for the Common Guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos), the Spiny Butterfly Ray (Gymnura altavela), the Common Stingray (Dasyatis pastinaca) and the Common Eagle Ray (Myliobatis aquila). Remarkably, these records indicate the annual presence of the once-though-extinct in the Western Mediterranean Common Guitarfish, with potentially pregnant females appearing in June and newborns in September. Additionally, further evidence is needed to confirm the occurrence of the Giant Guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) according to some reported pictures due to identification issues. These photographs suggest fisheries-induced mortality due to illegal retention and inadequate handling techniques is occurring to an unknown extent. Also, pregnant individuals and newborns of Spiny Butterfly Ray can be seen yearly throughout the summer, as well as potential aggregations of likely young-of-the-year of Common Stingray. Opportunistic scientific expeditions have further allowed us to document annual aggregations of 15-40 individuals of Common Eagle Ray with unknown function. These preliminary findings highlight the Murcia Eastern Coast as a potential conservation realm for highly endangered elasmobranch species. However, further research efforts are needed and warranted to inform effective management actions to ensure their survival.

title: Spatiotemporal distribution and sexual segregation in the Critically Endangered angelshark Squatina squatina in Spain’s largest marine reserve
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: Establishing how threatened wildlife are distributed spatially and temporally is essential for effective conservation and management planning. While many shark species are threatened globally, knowledge on sex-specific differences in behaviour and fine-scale habitat use remains limited, hindering the implementation of appropriate conservation actions. Here, acoustic telemetry was used to investigate sex-specific space use in the Critically Endangered angelshark Squatina squatina in the Canary Islands (Atlantic Ocean), a key stronghold for the species. We collected data on space use, residency and movement of adult males (n = 32) and females (n = 72) in Spain’s largest marine reserve (La Graciosa Marine Reserve) over 4 yr (2018−2022). Presence in offshore sites (>80 m depth) indicated long-term utilisation of deep-water habitat, not previously observed in this species. Males were more likely to be detected in deep water and displayed significantly greater levels of activity and roaming behaviour than females. Patterns of behaviour in shallow waters indicated both social and habitat sexual segregation. Diel variability was also recorded, with greater activity occurring nocturnally. This study demonstrates the importance of considering the spatiotemporal distribution of both sexes, horizontally and vertically, when designing effective conservation measures.
keywords: Acoustic telemetry; Angelshark; Conservation; Distribution; Spatial ecology

title: First records of critically endangered smoothback angel shark Squatina oculata Bonaparte 1840 and angelshark Squatina squatina (Linnaeus 1758) reproductive habitats in Türkiye, and over 50 new records demonstrating three Critical Angel Shark Areas (CASA’s)
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: In 2023, three records of angelshark stress-induced births onboard fishing vessels in Türkiye were recorded. The first record was from Fethiye Bay in January 2023, in which three Squatina oculata pups were aborted on the vessel, with one external yolk sac still attached, with the pups deceased pups. The second account was of five Squatina squatina pups aborted onboard a fishing vessel from the Dardanelles, in which all pups survived, and the last account was also from Fethiye Bay in March, 2023, this time in which three pups survived. This last account provides the only recent account on Squatina oculata reproduction from the last two decades. The pups were approximately 19.5 cm, 21.5 cm and 23 cm total length, with an internal yolk sac which could be seen iridescently through the body, estimated at about 3-4 cm in width. These records also provide important details of reproductive habitats, spawning grounds and spawning seasons, which seems to ocur in spring in Turkey. The data presents a new much smaller minimum maturity size for S. oculata. Also, data were summarized from citizen science records for Turkish sharks and rays along with other records directly from fishers providing a total of 51 previously unpublished angel shark records for Turkey, and highlighting three potential Critical Angel Shark Areas (CASAs) in Turkey; Fethiye Bay, Çanakkale Strait and Antalya Bay. We stress the need for better protection of these areas, along with scientific monitoring of these sites to learn more about these species.

title: Archival tagging reveals new insights in the horizontal and vertical movements of a critically endangered wedgefish
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: The smoothnose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus laevis) is a critically endangered shark-like ray that has received limited research attention. To address knowledge gaps in its behaviour and movement patterns, this study utilized satellite tagging over a 51-day period in the Arabian Gulf. Based on the resulting movement track, the specimen covered a minimum distance of 712 km, traversing the exclusive economic zones of three different countries. Its track began in the United Arab Emirates, from where it headed north, entering Iranian waters where it spent the majority of its time, before continuing westward across the Arabian Gulf and eventually reaching Qatari waters. Novel insights in its behaviour recorded a pattern of rapid ascent over the study period. Even though these ascents these ascents were observed both diurnal and nocturnal, they occurred predominately in the latter. Contrary to the prevailing belief that wedgefish are bottom-associated, the study animal spent a considerable amount of its time in the water column. Its use of a variety of depths in both nearshore and offshore waters highlights a potential susceptibility to multiple fishing year types. This underscores the need for an international, cooperative approach to the management and conservation of shark-like rays in the Arabian Gulf.

title: Cazón Project: Research to determine the true status of dogfish sharks in the Canary Islands
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: The Canary Islands, located in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa, have quickly become an idyllic place for elasmobranch species that inhabit their waters, primarily due to the absence of industrial fishing and the use of harmful fishing methods such as trawling. In the Canary Islands, fishing activities consist mainly of small-scale artisanal fishing and recreational fishing, which is gaining popularity and attracting more enthusiasts each year. However, sharks and rays are generally not targeted species in these fishing activities. Only dogfish sharks and various species within this family are intentionally fished or captured as bycatch in the islands. This is primarily due to the use of their meat for human consumption as "tollos", a typical food of the archipelago made with the dehydrated meat of these sharks. Currently, our knowledge of these species is limited to data derived from artisanal fishermen and their captures, which, as often is the case in many parts of the world, are underestimated due to poor or non-existent proper identification of each species. Including biological data (species, sexes) and/or ecological data (preferred areas, depths, or seasons), severely limiting their proper assessment or manage. In this study, the current status of these species in the Canary Islands is evaluated, aiming to identify the situation of each species as accurately as possible.
keywords: Elasmobranch; Fisheries; Endangered species; Archipelago

title: Coordinated Action for the Conservation of Critically Endangered Angel Sharks
session_name: Session 5: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 1)
abstract_text: The Angel Shark Project was established with the aim of securing the future of Critically Endangered angel sharks (Squatina squatina, S. aculeata and S. oculata) across the range. Among other regions, the Canary Islands, Wales, Libya, Greece, Corsica, Croatia and Ireland were identified as important and unique areas for at least one of the three angel shark species. The data gathered in these regions has contributed to the implementation of targeted conservation measures across the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea and to deliver priority policy outcomes across six countries. This two-way exchange of information between partners across the angel shark species’ ranges has been vital to better coordinate conservation action. This presentation will highlight some of the key milestones from the different regions, including enhancing legal protection in priority countries, co-developing regional action plans to minimise threats and promoting the sustainability of shark and ray fishing.

title: Re-launch of the Angel Shark Conservation Network: A community working to better protect angel sharks
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: The Angel Shark Conservation Network (ASCN) was established by the authors in 2016, to empower action to restore and safeguard angel shark populations throughout their natural range. To date, focusing on the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, which encompasses the range of three Critically Endangered angel shark species: Squatina aculeata, S. oculata, and S. squatina. The ASCN aims to facilitate dialogue and information sharing on angel shark conservation efforts and provides a mechanism for developing strategic conservation planning documents at different geographic scales. A number of Action Plans have been developed via multidisciplinary workshops, sitting underneath the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Angel Shark Conservation Strategy. These documents aim to identify the key actions needed to overcome major threats to angel sharks in each specific region to guide future research, management, policy, and conservation. Progress towards actions outlined in these documents will be discussed, highlighting how far we have come and what we have left to achieve. The ASCN actively encourages individuals and organisations to deliver actions outlined in the angel shark conservation planning documents, facilitating a collaborative approach, and working in partnership to support and deliver angel shark conservation. Various levels of ASCN membership exist, and recent work has been undertaken to better formalise this process. This presentation will outline the ASCN’s re-launch, with clearer guidance on how to get involved and hopes to expand the network to enable further action for angel sharks across their range. This work is funded by Shark Conservation Fund.

title: Utilizing human-wildlife Interaction data: A game-changer for guitarfish conservation
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: Human-wildlife interactions are crucial in shaping our understanding of nature and can significantly impact efforts to conserve endangered species and their habitats. As human activities continue to expand in the marine environment, encounters between humans and marine wildlife are expected to rise. Addressing and incorporating these interactions into conservation plans can provide valuable insights and bolster conservation efforts. In this study, we utilized the Marxan software to analyze data from the MECO citizen science project, focusing on two guitarfish species, the blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) and the common guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos), along the Mediterranean coast of Israel. Our objective was to identify areas of high probability for human encounters with guitarfish species while considering the specific activities conducted during these interactions. Our findings revealed that human activities varied across different areas during guitarfish encounters. By incorporating human activities as conservation targets in the Marxan analysis, in addition to guitarfish distribution data, we observed no significant shifts in the location of areas marked for conservation. However, the total area of these conservation zones increased significantly. This approach demonstrates how incorporating data on human-wildlife interactions can enhance conservation modeling efforts. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of including a social dimension in conservation planning, offering a fresh perspective on the process. By integrating human-wildlife interaction data, conservation strategies can be better tailored to specific locations and activities, facilitating more effective protection for guitarfish species and their habitats.
keywords: Human-wildlife interactions; Guitarfish; Conservation planning; Citizen science; Marxan

title: First campaign for the study of blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) in waters of Doñana National Park (Spain, North East Atlantic)
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: In June 2022, an initial expedition comprising members from the Fundación Oceanogràfic, Seville Aquarium, and LAMNA Association certified the presence of juvenile and adult 'guitarrón' or blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) within the protected waters of Doñana National Park in Huelva, Spain. These records confirmed previous non-published reports by researchers and data collected through the Mediterranean Elasmobranchs Citizen Observations (MECO) project. This could be the first indication of a stable population and a possible nursery area. Sampling was carried out on foot from Matalascañas to Guadalquivir river’s mouth (Sanlúcar de Barrameda) over a five-day period. A total of 14 specimens were observed, with estimations revealing 5 juveniles and 9 adults or subadults. Furthermore, suspicions about accidental catches by recreational and professional fishermen were also confirmed, through interviews with individuals on the beach who provided photos of these cases. More serious was the confirmation of the consumption of this protected species by the local population, a fact demonstrated through the interviews but also with the discovery of four severed heads on the beach itself, evidencing cases of poaching within Doñana’s marine protected area. The results of this expedition have provided hope for a larger study of the area, to be conducted during the years 2023-2026, allowing for the creation of a catch and release program and the obtention of DNA samples. Further collaborations on these efforts are welcomed.
keywords: Glaucostegidae; Glaucostegus cemiculus; Habitat; Poaching; Protected areas

title: Detecting the presence of elasmobranchs in Wales using environmental DNA
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: Environmental DNA (eDNA) methodologies allow us to assess biodiversity by taking samples from the environment (e.g water, sediment or air) and extracting DNA from the samples to identify the presence of species. We designed an eDNA survey to gather information on elasmobranch presence in the Carmarthen Bay and Estuaries (CBAE) Special Area of Conservation (SAC) in South Wales. Sampling sites were informed using hydrodynamic and tracer modelling based on residual patterns, led by Bangor University. Water samples were taken from 10 sites across CBAE SAC each month, for 12 months. These data were brought together with samples taken in 2020/2021 by Angel Shark Project: Wales, which covered 10 sites across 12 months in the Pen Llyn A’r Sarnau (PLAS) SAC in North Wales. Further samples were taken and analysed concurrently with BRUVS surveys in the PLAS SAC. A total of eleven elasmobranch species were detected across the two SACs, including all four Project SIARC focal species – angelshark, common stingray, spurdog and tope. This presentation will highlight the key findings from these surveys. Project SIARC is a collaboration between the Zoological Society of London, Natural Resources Wales and six partners and made possible thanks to the National Lottery Heritage Fund, Welsh Government’s Nature Networks Fund and On the EDGE Conservation.

title: The cradle of diversity: Central Atlantic Ocean hides a mosaic of skate species (Rajiformes)
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: Skates (Rajiformes) represent one of the most intriguing cases of high species richness coupled with extremely conservative morphological and ecological traits. Small differences are described within and between species and increasing cases of cryptic speciation have been recorded among sister and non-sister taxa. More interestingly, this condition has been frequently observed in Central Atlantic Ocean (CAO), along the coasts of Western Africa, between Angola and Senegal, where oceanographic heterogeneities such as current systems, may play a key role for ecological speciation in skates. The use of multiple mtDNA loci and its integration with nuDNA microsatellite has been successfully applied to estimate the genetic variation in skate species inhabiting the CAO. Phylogenetic reconstructions, phylogeographic patterns and genetic connectivity estimates were applied to test the hypothesis that restricted gene flow and genetic divergence within Raja species reflect known climate and bio-oceanographic discontinuities. The widely distributed Raja miraletus species complex counts five deeply distinct lineages three of which co-occur in CAO: the Angolan Raja cf. miraletus, the Senegalese and sympatric R. parva and Raja cf. miraletus. In addition, an ancient, hidden lineage nesting in the clade Raja straeleni/R. clavata/R. maderensis was identified in Angola. The complexity of oceanographic system acting in the CAO (i.e., the Benguela Current region and the intertropical Canary current inflowing from the northeast) may have influenced the diversification of the Angolan and Senegalese taxa, boosting the biodiversity of the area, in an unprecedented anthology of species-specific evolutionary histories.
keywords: cryptic species; hidden lineages; Raja; mtDNA; nuDNA

title: Common stingray's (Dasyatis pastinaca) first recorded and studied nursery area in Greece
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: Elasmobranchs, including the common stingray, are pivotal components of marine ecosystems, yet much remains to be understood about their habitat requirements and life history characteristics. The identification and investigation of nursery areas are critical for effective conservation and management, as these areas offer essential resources for the early life stages, contributing significantly to population sustainability. A nursery area of Common stingrays has been discovered in Liri Beach in 2018, on the eastern coast of central Greece. Adults and juveniles have been recorded at depths of 3 to 6 meters depth on a sandy soil bed. By employing field surveys, we have explored the presence and attributes of the common stingray's nursery area in the region. Our findings unveil a shallow, nearshore region that provides optimal environmental conditions for the growth and development of juvenile stingrays. These habitats afford protection against predation and facilitate access to abundant food resources, ensuring the successful survival and subsequent recruitment of young individuals into the adult population. Furthermore, we have examined the ecological interactions and connectivity between the identified nursery area in Central Greece and the surrounding habitats, underscoring the significance of considering broader ecological networks for effective conservation planning. By comprehending the spatial dynamics and connectivity patterns, we can devise strategies to safeguard and manage these critical areas, securing the long-term viability of the common stingray population.
keywords: Common stingray; Dasyatis pastinaca; Nursery area

title: Geographical distribution influences the accumulation of metals in the liver and muscle of Squatina squatina
session_name: Session 6: Threatened elasmobranchs in coastal waters (Part 2)
abstract_text: The Canary Islands was identified as a unique stronghold for the Angel shark (Squatina squatina), a species considered Critically Endangered according to the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Angelsharks inhabit coastal and shallow areas, being exposed to the effects of anthropogenic pollution, such as the accumulation of heavy metals. In this study, we analysed the concentration of twenty-one metals and trace elements in liver and muscle samples from dead specimens, nine from the Canary Islands and five from the Celtic Seas region (Wales and Ireland), using optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), cold vapor atomic absorption spectroscopy (CV-AAS), and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The results did not show sex as an influential factor in the concentration of heavy metals in the Canarian population. However, the size and weight of individuals were negatively correlated with Hg, Mo, B, and Cr in muscle, and positively correlated with Co, Fe, V, Mn, and Cr in the liver. These differences were more pronounced in a prenatal individual. The results indicate that growth may play a crucial role in the bioaccumulation and biomagnification of metals in organs. In terms of geographical distribution, we observed significant differences between the individuals from the Canary Islands and the Celtic Seas regarding the concentration of Hg, Cd, and Cr, which were higher in the Canary Islands, and Zn and Mn, which were higher in the Celtic Seas, likely due to differences in pollution levels between the two areas.
keywords: Squatina squatina; Heavy metals; Bioaccumulation; Muscle; Liver

title: Evaluating the historical abundance trends of large sharks in the Pelagie Archipelago using Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK)
session_name: Session 7: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 1)
abstract_text: According to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), around 50% of shark and ray species are facing high risk of extinction in the Mediterranean Sea. To date, the knowledge of elasmobranchs is fragmented and focused for certain species and areas of the basin with poor population assessment, especially in remote sites. The Pelagie Archipleago (Pelagie islands), is considered one of the most important hot-spot for sharks in the Mediterranean Sea. This area hosts a wide range of species potentially threatened by historical fishing pressure and habitat loss, especially large-bodied sharks, whose spatiotemporal patterns of abundance and distribution are poorly known. Evaluating historical dynamics of cartilaginous fish in the Pelagie archipelago can be very challenging and it can be crucial to understand their current population status. In the present study, we used LEK (Local Ecological Knowledge) through the historical memory and experience of fishers to collect information about the elasmobranch species inhabiting the Pelagie islands, with a particular focus of large-bodied sharks. Based on fishers’ perception, we recorded a dramatic reduction of large pelagic sharks over 60 years, mainly hammerheads (Sphyrna spp.) and sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus). We also reconstructed the historical abundance of several elasmobranchs inhabiting the area. Our results provide important insights that can be used as a baseline for conservation initiatives in a shark data-poor region such as the Pelagie Archipelago.
