title: Heavy metal concentrations in muscle tissue of chondrichthyans from the western Mediterranean Sea: the tip of the iceberg
session_name: Session 7: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 1)
abstract_text: The western Mediterranean Sea is a region with a high diversity of chondrichthyan species; however, this region is subjected to a high discharge of pollutants, such as heavy metals. Consequently, owing to their ecological role, these species are prone to heavy metal bioaccumulation. Therefore, an assessment of the concentrations of three heavy metals present in the muscle tissue of 17 chondrichthyan species in the western Mediterranean Sea was performed. A total of 116 individuals were used, mainly caught by trawling and small-scale fishing. Lead (Pb), cadmium (Cd), and copper (Cu) were quantified using Microwave-Assisted Extraction (MAE) and Graphite Furnace Atomic Absorption Spectrometry (GF-AAS). Significant differences were observed between some species and taxonomic groups for Pb, Cd, and Cu. Among all the analysed species, the rabbit fish (Chimaera monstrosa) presented the highest concentration (mg/kg wet weight) of Pb (0.2924 ± 0.1689), of which some individuals exceeded the concentration threshold for Pb established by the Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915. However, the velvet belly lanternshark (Etmopterus spinax) had the highest concentrations (mg/kg wet weight) of Cd (0.0622 ± 0.0244) and Cu (0.8179 ± 0.4167), exceeding the maximum concentration of Cd allowed by the (EU) 2023/915. A negative correlation between the concentration of Pb and trophic level was found, owing to the high concentrations found in low-trophic level species, such as C. monstrosa and E. spinax. Overall, the results obtained are important for human consumption. This is because these species are consumed and of great commercial interest in this region.
keywords: Chondrichthyans; Heavy metals; Marine pollution; western Mediterranean Sea; Human consumption

title: Heavy metal monitoring via the small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula; Linnaeus, 1758): Biomonitor potential assesment & multiple-scenario implementation
session_name: Session 7: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 1)
abstract_text: The small-spotted catshark Scyliorhinus canicula, is a demersal Scyliorhinid shark species commonly found in Mediterranean and Northeastern Atlantic waters. The philopatric and sedentary nature of adult female individuals, along with its high abundance among bottom trawl bycatch; stock exploitation resilience and widespread distribution could support the xenobiotic biomonitoring potential of this species. Previous research on the subject concluded the specie´s muscle tissue is capable of reflecting space-time persistent Pb, Cd and Cu hotspots. To further explore such potential, interspecific monitoring has been attempted between Merluccius merluccius and S. canicula for which a total of 49 individuals of each species were gathered and data correlation was performed among individuals captured in the same haul. The Cd and Pb biomonitor potential of S. canicula egg capsules was also assessed. A total of 75 embryos were exposed via solution to different concentration ranges of these xenobiotics (Cd = 0.05-17.12 and Pb = 3-102.78 mg·Kg-1) for a 2.5 month period. All samples were analysed via GFAAS and matrices were digested via MAE techniques. High significant interspecific correlation values were observed in Cd and Pb concentrations between both species (Spearman r = 0.817 and 0.833 respectively) as well as moderate positive correlation for Cu (Spearman r = 0.633). Regarding Pb and Cd accumulation by egg capsules, high linearity was observed between dissolved concentrations of the elements and those found within the egg capsule (r2 = 0.98 and 0.96 respectively) with signifficant differences between trials occurring at higher Cd and Pb exposure concentrations.

title: Microplastics in reef manta ray feeding grounds
session_name: Session 7: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 1)
abstract_text: Microplastics (plastic particles sized under 5mm) are ubiquitous in the marine environment. They are known to have negative effects on marine organisms when ingested, including accumulation in digestive systems, causing starvation, and leaching of toxic chemicals, impacting development and reproduction. The habitat of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi), a filter-feeding elasmobranch, overlaps with plastic pollution hotspots globally. This makes them at risk of ingesting the particles, with potential negative consequences on their fitness. The species is already listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red list, due to other anthropogenic pressures, such as fishing. It is therefore important to understand the risk of plastic pollution on this charismatic megafaunal species. This study is investigating the presence of microplastics in reef manta ray feeding grounds in the Chagos Archipelago. This is a no-take Marine Protected Area, home to a resident population of reef manta rays. However remote, the beaches of the Archipelago are covered in plastic debris which originates from elsewhere. This suggests there will be plenty of microplastics in the Archipelago waters. Quantifying the amount of microplastic in the water will build a better picture of how it could impact the local population of reef manta rays. It will also hopefully input into wider conversations about plastic reduction on remote islands.
keywords: Microplastics; filter-feeder; manta ray; pollution

title: Metabolism, biogeography, and range shifts in sharks & rays
session_name: Session 8: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 2)
abstract_text: Environmental temperature affects physiological functions, representing a barrier for the range expansions of ectothermic species. To understand the link between thermal physiology and biogeography, a key question is whether among-species thermal sensitivity of metabolic rates is mechanistically constrained or buffered through physiological remodeling over evolutionary time. The former conception, the Universal Temperature Dependence hypothesis, predicts similar among- and within-species thermal sensitivity. The latter conception, the Metabolic Cold Adaptation hypothesis, predicts lower among-species thermal sensitivity than within-species sensitivity. Previous studies that tested these hypotheses for fishes overwhelmingly investigated teleosts with elasmobranchs understudied. Here, we show that among-species thermal sensitivity of resting metabolic rates is lower than within-species sensitivity in teleosts but not in elasmobranchs. Further, species richness declines with latitude more rapidly in elasmobranchs than in teleosts. Metabolic Cold Adaptation exhibited by teleosts might underpin their high diversity at high latitudes, whereas the inflexible thermal sensitivity approximated by Universal Temperature Dependence of elasmobranchs might explain their low diversity at high latitudes. These findings are discussed in the context of range expansions of sharks and rays, including recent examples from Ireland and the UK.
keywords: Range shifts; Metabolism; Thermal sensitivity

title: Shifts in the habitat suitability for large hammerhead sharks under climate change
session_name: Session 8: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 2)
abstract_text: One of the chief consequences of climate change is the worldwide redistribution of species in the pursue of physiologically and ecologically favourable conditions. As part of one of the most threatened groups of vertebrates, assessing how climate change may affect the distribution patterns of key shark species is essential for their long-term conservation and management. The present study aims to assess how climate change projections (based on the representative concentration pathways 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, and 8.5) for the middle and end of the century may affect the global patterns of habitat suitability (HS) for large hammerhead sharks – a unique and particularly threatened groups of elasmobranchs. Poleward shifts are projected for all three species, with considerable tropical declines for both S. lewini and S. zygaena. Additionally, regional shifts in suitability have the potential to affect population connectivity, the access to key habitats, and levels of exposure to other anthropogenic pressures, along with the effectiveness of conservation and management efforts. Our results showcase the importance of climate change for species’ extinction risk assessment and the urgency of its consideration for the design and implementation of conservation measures tailored to the oceans of tomorrow.
keywords: Ecological niche models; habitat suitability; hammerhead sharks; Climate change

title: Northeast Atlantic elasmobranch community on the move: functional reorganisation in response to climate change
session_name: Session 8: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 2)
abstract_text: While spatial distribution shifts have been documented in many marine fishes under global change, the responses of elasmobranchs have rarely been studied, despite their irreplaceable role in the ecosystems and their high extinction risk, which may have led to an underestimation of their potential additional threats. We used a 24-year-long time series (1997-2020) of scientific bottom trawl surveys to examine the effects of climate change on the spatial distribution of nine elasmobranch species within Northeast Atlantic waters. We found that suitable habitats for four species increased on average by a factor of 1.6 and, for six species, shifted northwestwards and/or in depth over the past two decades. By integrating species traits, we showed changes in habitat suitability led to changes in the elasmobranchs trait-composition. Moreover, communities deepened and their mean trophic level decreased. We also note an increase in the mean community size at maturity correlated in a less pronounced way to a decrease in fecundity. Because skates and sharks are functionally unique and dangerously vulnerable to both climate change and fishing, we advocate for urgent considerations of species traits in management measures because of their utility to better identify species whose loss could have irreversible impacts in face of the myriad of upcoming threats, especially for unmonitored species. In this way, we would gain efficiency in implementing biodiversity conservation.
keywords: climate change; community; elasmobranch; species traits; shift

title: Resilience of juvenile sharks to disease under moderate marine heat wave conditions
session_name: Session 8: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 2)
abstract_text: Climate change is affecting the oceans in different ways. Marine heat waves, for example, are becoming more frequent, more prolonged, and more intense, endangering marine life. Assessing the impact of these extreme events on disease outbreak and dynamics in sharks is poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of a simulated (moderate) marine heat wave (MHW; Δ2°C; 9 days) on the physiological (ventilation rates) and biochemical (several oxidative-stress biomarkers on gills, muscle, brain, and liver tissues) condition of juvenile small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) infected with ectoparasite Amyloodinium ocellatum. No mortality differences were observed, but a significant increase in ventilation rates were observed under the MHW treatment. Significant changes in enzymatic antioxidant activities were observed among tissues, but only superoxide dismutase activity was affected under MHW conditions. Protein repair and removal mechanisms (heat shock protein and total ubiquitin), and oxidative damage on lipids (malondialdehyde) and DNA (8-hydroxy-2′- deoxyguanosine) also did not significantly change between treatments. Our result is consistent with other studies that have shown that sharks display some level of resilience to the effects of climate change-related stressors. However, another category of marine heat wave (IV or V for example) could produce other physiological effects.
keywords: Climate change; Elasmobranch; Parasite; Oxidative stress

title: A social science story: what motivates recreational shark angling in the UK?
session_name: Session 8: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 2)
abstract_text: The role of recreational angling as both a threat to shark stocks and an opportunity to support shark conservation tends to be overlooked. Sharks have been described as the aquatic ‘big game’ equivalent, displayed as ‘trophies’ and caught for the ‘thrill of the fight’. Historical fears of sharks have led to an increase in shark fishing tournaments, increasing the rate of decline of shark populations threatened with extinction. However, modern-day social science studies in the United States and Australia have contradicted these fears, with a growing desire amongst anglers to become advocates for shark conservation. Here, we examine anglers’ motivations behind shark fishing in the United Kingdom (UK) a popular but understudied location for recreational shark fishing. Angler demographics, perceptions towards sharks and perceptions of shark population trends were also explored. A total of seven shark fishing operators and 44 recreational anglers responded to our structured surveys throughout Aug-Nov 2021. Respondents primarily comprised of over-fifty, educated and wealthy male anglers. Anglers were motivated by the ‘appreciation for sharks and nature’ (n=43) and the ‘thrill/challenge’ (n=38). Obtaining a photo (status) was the least popular reason for taking part in shark fishing, further contradicting historical studies. Recreational shark fishing in the UK is strictly catch and release, with anglers demonstrating best practice techniques to minimise stress to caught sharks. We also identify a population of anglers who are knowledgeable about local shark species and recognise their role in contributing to shark conservation but identify a lack of higher-level management to legislate change.
keywords: Recreational fisheries; Social science; Fisheries management; Blue sharks; Conservation

title: A review of elasmobranch catch-and-release science: synthesis of current knowledge, implications for best practice and future research directions
session_name: Session 8: Other anthropogenic pressures - contaminants, climate change and recreation (Part 2)
abstract_text: Until relatively recently commercial fisheries have been considered the main driving factor for elasmobranch population declines. However, this belief has begun to shift with the realisation that recreational elasmobranch catches may equal or exceed commercial catches in some regions. Many recreational angling fisheries for elasmobranchs involve high participation in catch-and-release angling practices. However, high release rates may not necessarily equate to high survival rates. Therefore, to assist accurate assessment of the potential impact of recreational angling on elasmobranchs, we attempted to summarise and integrate currently available information on specific risk factors associated with recreational angling, alongside associated mortality rates, as well as information on angler behaviour as it relates to identified risk factors. We categorised the major angling-related effects into two groups: injury-induced effects; and biochemical disruption-induced effects; providing a summary of each group and outlining the main lethal and sub-lethal outcomes stemming from these. These outcomes include post-release mortality, behavioural recovery periods (which may in-turn confer increased predation risks), chronic health impacts, and capture-induced parturition and abortion. Additionally, we detailed a range of angling practices and equipment, including hook-type, hook removal and emersion, as well as inter- and intra-specific factors, including aerobic scope, respiratory mode, body size and species-specific behaviours, which may influence injury and/or mortality rates and should therefore be considered when assessing angling-related impacts. We then utilised these data to provide a range of actionable recommendations for both anglers and policymakers which would serve to reduce the population-level impact of recreational angling on these enigmatic animals.
keywords: Recreational angling; Rod and line; Lamniformes; Carcharhiniformes; Rajiformes

title: Use of CT scan reveals necropsy-overlooked swordfish (Xiphias gladius) impalement injuries in stranded blue sharks (Prionace glauca)
session_name: Theme topic: Elasmobranch stranding events: what can we learn?
abstract_text: Recently, analysis of eighteen strandings in eastern Spain has identified fourteen lethal interactions between blue sharks and swordfish. In these cases, the sharks were impaled in the cephalic region by swordfish rostra. While some signs of interaction were easily identifiable, others proved elusive despite thorough physical examinations and dissection on necropsy. Computed Tomography (CT) has emerged as a valuable diagnostic tool for identifying and characterizing these distinctive injuries, even revealing healed wounds from previous impalements. The detailed imagery obtained enables the evaluation of tissue damage and wound trajectory, offering a unique insight into each interaction. We show the efficiency of this technique by using a Somatom Volume Access (Siemens) scanner located at the Oceanogràfic veterinary hospital. Parameters for body exploration included a 5 mm slice thickness and interval, with a retro-recon acquisition of 0.5 mm utilizing lung and mediastinal algorithms. Rostra fragments were discovered embedded in soft tissues or cranial cartilage in twelve sharks, four of which have multiple rostra from past impalements. Two other animals exhibited signs of impalement without fragments. Analysis of the cases always shows adult sharks impaled by juvenile swordfish. The high prevalence (77.8%) and similarity of the interactions diminish the likelihood of chance accidents, suggesting intentional ofensive or defensive behaviour by the swordfish. These data suggest that agonistic interactions between swordfish and blue sharks may be more common than previously thought Due to challenges in lesion detection, impalement may have been overlooked in the past, highlighting the importance of employing CT scans whenever possible.
keywords: Behaviour; Interspecific relations; Agonistic interactions; Causes of Stranding; Diagnostic Tools

title: What do the lesions found in stranded blue sharks (Prionace glauca) reveal about their interactions with swordfish (Xiphias gladius)
session_name: Theme topic: Elasmobranch stranding events: what can we learn?
abstract_text: Fatal interactions between blue sharks (Prionace glauca) and swordfishes (Xiphias gladius) have been described in the western Mediterranean Sea as a cause of stranding and death of the former in the last years. This study describes, both macroscopic and microscopically, the lesions found in eight blue sharks, stranded in Spanish coasts, presenting evidence of impalement from swordfish´s rostrum. All the analysed animals presented the fatal injuries in the head, mainly grouped around the eyes in the frontal plane. Injures were characterized by multiple haemorrhages, predominant heterophilic cell infiltrates, and the presence of fibrin in the fatal injury, which are typical signs of an acute lesion. The most affected tissue was the brain, which showed meningeal and brain haemorrhage, accompanied by encephalitis and encephalomalacia. Additionally, we observed lesions in some eyes that were stabbed, displaying acute panophthalmitis. Furthermore, chronic signs such as the presence of fibroblasts and mononuclear infiltrates in the wounds, as well as rostrums from past interactions completely surrounded by fibrotic connective tissue, were clear indications of past interactions that had healed. These findings suggest that sharks have the potential to survive these types of interactions. The animals showing signs of chronicity exhibited other lesions repeatedly, such as hepatic emaciation, necrotic haemorrhagic ulcers with mononuclear infiltrates in the spiral valve, and enlargement of the renal glomerulus. The complete necropsy and study of the tissues of the stranded sharks proved to be a useful tool to better understand the nature and the consequences of the interaction between these two species.
keywords: Agonistic interactions; Stranding causes; Veterinary; Pathology; Necropsy procedures

title: Below the surface of the Welsh coast using BRUVS
session_name: Session 9: Citizen science II: Citizen scientists collecting novel samples or data
abstract_text: Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS) are widely used as a non-destructive electronic tool to investigate the abundance and diversity of fish in marine and freshwater environments. Project SIARC is working with local fishers and their charter vessels to deploy BRUVS off the coast of North Wales to obtain footage that improves our understanding of species, including elasmobranchs present in North Wales and their habitat utilisation. So far, from 90 BRUV deployments, 41 different fish species have been recorded, including five elasmobranchs. This presentation will highlight the key findings from the first year of BRUVS deployment. In parallel, the footage obtained from the BRUVS allows us to make life under the Welsh waters visible to citizen scientists globally. Video footage captured is shared via Instant Wild (an online tool that allows the general public to identify wildlife species from remote camera footage across the world), allowing individuals to identify species, contributing to data collection and increasing awareness of the elasmobranchs present in Welsh waters whilst enhancing inclusivity and access of the natural environment. Project SIARC is a collaboration between the Zoological Society of London, Natural Resources Wales and six partners and made possible thanks to the National Lottery Heritage Fund, Welsh Government’s Nature Networks Fund and On the EDGE Conservation.

title: Tourism-led monitoring of a migratory oceanic shark in the UK
session_name: Session 9: Citizen science II: Citizen scientists collecting novel samples or data
abstract_text: Monitoring pelagic highly migratory species is challenging, particularly in regions where weather conditions can be unpredictable and adverse. The blue shark Prionace glauca is no exception, and recent estimates of ~10M individuals fished annually, understanding their distribution and habitat preference is important for area-based management. Blue shark swim-with tourism is increasing across various countries, including the UK, providing both a need to understand the nature of these interactions, and an opportunity to gather novel data on this highly migratory species. UK tour operators reported blue shark interaction data 2021-2023, maxN, swimmer numbers and environmental parameters. Further data were obtained on tidal state, depth, SST, and chlorophyll-a concentration. Chum soak time and maxN were used as response variables to understand the drivers of shark occurrence and relative abundance. Preliminary results show that tidal phase, sea surface temperature and depth are likely to be important factors influencing blue shark occurrence, distribution and relative abundance. This study provides not only a unique insight into the ecology and behaviour of a globally important shark species, but has also created a valuable opportunity for ongoing collaboration between science and industry, and a springboard for long-term data collection and active management of a growing blue economy sector.

title: First porbeagle shark photo-Identification catalogue: free diving and social science to enhance ecological knowledge Lamna nasus off Brittany costs (France)
session_name: Session 9: Citizen science II: Citizen scientists collecting novel samples or data
abstract_text: Photo identification is a non-invasive method used to distinguish individuals in the wild based on some external visual criterium. As a capture-recapture methodology photo-ID allows to evaluate important ecological parameters such as spatio-temporal preferences, philopatry, abundance up to growth rates estimation. Porbeagle shark has encountered a severe decrease all other its range of distribution and was subject to a fishing regulation by European Council (No 23/2010); since that access to biological information on the species is scarce. DRDH team started in 2021 a free diving protocol to follow hotspots of porbeagle (Lamna nasus) established in the northern cost of Brittany. A data set of videos and photos was gathered through regular standardized dives from DRDH team as well as social media and stakeholder inquiries. We defined 5 different phenotypic marks which allow us to identify more than 100 individual sharks and thus initiate the first and build up a working catalog. Sightings occurred from may to October between 2015 and 2023 with some re sightings confirmed within weeks, months or years distance. All encountered sharks were females, ranging from 1,5 to 3 meters Lt documented for their maturity status. The initial results of this study support the ecological importance of the area for the species in regards to biotic and abiotic parameters. The participatory science dimension of the project offers interesting public awareness possibilities in addition to data provisioning and collaborative tool for other international research teams. Outputs will be discussed in the context of a growing interest for shark and underwater tourism.
keywords: Photo-ID; Porbeagle shark; Conservation; Free-diving; Tourism

title: Mobulids in the Canary Islands: what do we know?
session_name: Session 9: Citizen science II: Citizen scientists collecting novel samples or data
abstract_text: Despite the charismatic status of the Mobulidae family, our current understanding of this group remains limited. Given their highly migratory nature and the current global vulnerability they face, it is imperative to gain a comprehensive understanding of their ecology and behaviour in order to support conservation actions. Up until now, there has been a significant knowledge gap in mobulid research in the Canary Islands. Situated in the Eastern Atlantic, the Canary Islands offer unique opportunities for studying these animals. Manta Catalog represents the first line of work focused on the Mobulidae family in the region. Through community science, engaging the fishing and diving sectors, and by reviewing historical sources of information, we have compiled baseline information on the occurrence of this group in the archipelago. This work significantly contributes to our knowledge on these threatened animals in the Canary Islands and emphasises the importance of community science in long-term studies of migratory and pelagic species.

title: The egg case: Successful extraction of DNA from beached egg cases enables elasmobranch genetic diversity assessment
session_name: Session 9: Citizen science II: Citizen scientists collecting novel samples or data
abstract_text: Most elasmobranch populations are under pressure, and to advise policy makers on appropriate conservation measures, data on abundance, life history traits, spawning grounds and population structure are required. The application of DNA based techniques can provide some of this information, but commonly is dependent on tissue sampling (e.g., muscle, scale and blood) which requires handling and potentially underestimate less common species. Environmental DNA (eDNA) is shown as a reliable tool for the assessment of elasmobranch species diversity, but so far is unable to provide reliable data on population diversity. Egg cases of oviparous elasmobranchs can form a valuable aid in determining a species spatial distribution, defining spawning areas and DNA based analysis of population structure. So far, egg cases for this type of research were collected from both commercial fisheries and scientific surveys, generally with the embryo still inside, ensuring the quality of DNA. However, many of the egg cases wash up on shore after hatching departure or predation. When exposed to the elements, the genetic material in the egg case will start degrading, but DNA fragments of sufficient quality could still be viable for population genetics. We now present the successful isolation and sequencing of 2kb long mtDNA fragments from 14-day-old, hatched egg cases using a combination of liquid nitrogen, keratinase and collagenase. Developing this method further, beached egg cases collected by means of citizen science can provide a useful tool to determine oviparous elasmobranch population structure with limited resources and the added bonus of creating public awareness.
keywords: egg cases; population genetics; oviparous; mtDNA; elasmobranch

title: Are deep-sea chimaeras a hidden conservation priority we've ignored?
abstract_text: Deep-sea chondrichthyans have been underestimated and overshadowed. This misconception assumes they are unaffected by global changes and face minimal fishing threats. Among chondrichthyans, the order Chimaeriformes, specifically the rabbitfish Chimaera monstrosa, is one of the most striking examples. Our three-year research focused on unravelling the mysteries surrounding C. monstrosa in the Northeast Atlantic, where it is commonly caught as bycatch. It is classified as 'Near Threatened' by IUCN in European waters. Although we documented its abundance, habitat preferences, and responses to warming waters, significant gaps persist in understanding its life history traits and ecology, hindering targeted conservation measures. Using models and mapping tools, our study aimed to identify diverse populations and critical areas in need of protection. Along the Norwegian coast, we observed variations in growth rates and maturity, indicating potential adaptations to fisheries or environmental conditions. We located some areas that could arguably function as mating or nursery areas. Our research suggests that the newly colonized waters of northern Norway host a well-developed population of C. monstrosa. This colonization and potential further expansion northward, driven by warmer waters, underscore the necessity for monitoring critical areas, vulnerability to warming waters, and potential changes in the food web, particularly in the warming and heavily impacted North Sea. By providing insights into C. monstrosa's distribution patterns, regional variations, and implications for conservation, these findings contribute to the development of species-specific conservation measures.

title: Exploration of management strategies for a sustainable fishery of elasmobranchs in the Adriatic Sea
abstract_text: High bycatch of elasmobranchs and their decline in the Adriatic Sea call for management actions. Within the Italian monitoring programs of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, we investigated the post-release survival rates of juveniles of commercial species to explore the efficacy and feasibility of the implementation of a minimum conservation reference size (MCRS). From May 2020 to June 2023, through 90 on-board fishing trips using different fishing gears we evaluated the At-Vessel Mortality (AVM; 3443 individuals, 14 species), Short-term post-release mortality (St-PRM; two hours after capture, on board, 788 individuals, 14 species) and Long-term PRM (Lt-PRM; 72 hours after capture, at laboratory, 121 individuals, 3 species). AMV was on average 16%, varying among species, fishing gears and seasons and depending on factors such as temperature and duration of air exposure. St-PRM and Lt-PRM were generally low, below 16% and 20%, respectively. To better estimate mortality, by combining conventional tagging and acoustic telemetry, in the framework of the MedBycatch project, we investigated Lt-PRM in the field. We tagged 1816 individuals of 16 species with spaghetti tags, 61 individuals of 3 species with acoustic tags. The tagging study contributed also to the understanding of the use of space and to highlight residency and site fidelity behaviours. To rigorously explore the potential efficacy and sustainability of the release of juveniles, we constructed individual based population dynamics models to assess the expected recovery of populations according to different MCRS and survival rates.

title: By ElasmoCatch: a multidisciplinary approach to improve knowledge and conservation of elasmobranchs in Amvrakikos Gulf
abstract_text: The poor conservation status of Chondrichthyes in the Mediterranean Sea requires effective management strategies. Ad-hoc conservation measures for different areas and species are needed. In this perspective, the By ElasmoCatch Project is focusing on the Amvrakikos Gulf (Greece). Here, only small-scale fishery is operating, using set-nets and longlines, in some cases targeting Mustelus mustelus and Myliobatidae. From 2022 until now, 547 fishing operations have been monitored through interviews (532) and onboard surveys (45). A total of 1176 elasmobranchs have been recorded. Among the 10 species present, 2 Critically Endangered (Mediterranean Region) stingrays Aetomylaeus bovinus and Gymnura altavela were commonly caught (25.5% of recorded elasmobranchs). Moreover, identification issues for specimens of the family Dasyatidae emerged. To better understand the biology and ecology of elasmobranchs in the area and clearly identify the species, a multidisciplinary approach is used (e.g., data on life-history traits, stomach contents, genetic). Finally, we are investigating post-release mortality (through 40 minutes tank maintenance, 92; and a conventional-tagging program, 189) to understand the efficacy of release as a management strategy. Given the high biodiversity and presence of both pregnant females and newborns of different species, this region appears to be crucial for elasmobranchs, and it was proposed as Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA). Future steps will include an acoustic-tagging program to further understand survival after capture and use of space, heavy-metal analyses, and testing of other mitigation measures (e.g., gear modifications), with the final aim to find the best management strategy and its implementation by the local community.

title: Enhancing Elasmobranch Mitogenomic Knowledge: Transcriptome-Based Assembly Approach
abstract_text: Commonly, there is a shortage of available omics resources from elasmobranchs on public databases, such as genomes, transcriptomes, and mitogenomes. This highlights the importance of taking the most advantage of available resources. Thus, we assessed the potential of using transcriptomes from elasmobranchs to computationally recover their mitogenomes. Within this work, we gathered more than 30 transcriptomic entries from the NCBI Database from elasmobranch species whose mitogenome was not available. We were able to perform mitochondrial genome assemblies for 10 species whose mitogenome was previously unreported: Isistius brasiliensis, Negaprion brevirostris, Potamotrygon amandae, P. leopoldi, Rhizoprionodon taylori, R. terraenovae, Scyliorhinus rotifer, Squalus suckleyi, Tetronarce californica, and Urobatis jamaicensis. The recovered assemblies ranged from 16,620 to 17,710 nucleotides, and half of the final assemblies presented a 100% recovery rate (the lowest reached 92%). The assembly of these mitogenomes will empower further studies that can be relevant to understanding the evolutionary and ecological framework of elasmobranchs, especially considering the important role of the mitochondrial genes on oxidative phosphorylation. Additionally, it will assist population genomic studies that often rely on partial mitochondrial genomes, extending the already powerful tool of transcriptomics.
keywords: Mitogenomes; Transcriptomics; Bioinformatics

title: Survival and post-release behaviour of pelagic sharks caught in recreational catch-and-release fisheries in Europe revealed by electronic tagging
abstract_text: Recreational shark fishing accounts for millions of shark captures each year across the world, with many fishers now employing a "catch and release" (C&R) approach. In Europe, C&R fisheries for sharks are widespread and involve thousands of sharks each year, including the blue shark (Prionace glauca) and the porbeagle shark (Lamna nasus). Despite this, studies on the potential impacts of C&R fishing are generally lacking, with only one investigation conducted on porbeagle sharks in North America and none on blue sharks globally. To address the potential impacts of a range of handling and environmental conditions, this ongoing study uses short-term electronic tags (45 days) to assess the effects of C&R fishing on the behaviour and mortality of blue and porbeagle sharks caught recreationally in southwest UK waters and the northern Adriatic Sea. To date, no mortalities have been observed among tagged sharks (n=18). However, high-resolution data obtained from retrieved tags (n=5) suggests differences in diving patterns between the immediate post-release period and later stages of tracking, indicating a potential behavioural impact of capture. These preliminary results suggest that, within the range of handling and environmental conditions studied so far, C&R fishing for blue and porbeagle sharks is unlikely to results in mortality with 45 days of release, although sublethal short-term effects on animal welfare may require further attention. Further research is necessary to examine the short- and long-term behavioural effects of C&R fishing and identify specific aspects of the practice that may be refined to improve outcomes for sharks.
keywords: angling; catch and release; telemetry; conservation; ecology

title: Filling the gap: conservation genetics of the Sicklefin devil ray - from oceanic islands to ocean basins
abstract_text: The survival of chondrichthyans is a major marine conservation concern, with over one-third of species currently at risk of extinction due to their exceptional vulnerability and low resilience to high levels of exploitation. However, our extremely limited knowledge of their basic ecology hampers the implementation of proper management and conservation actions. There is also a knowledge gap on the genetic diversity and population structure of these species at different spatial scales. This is especially true for migratory species, such as the Sicklefin devil ray (Mobula tarapacana), that utilizes the restricted coastal habitats of oceanic islands. Understanding the degree of genetic connectivity allows to define population boundaries and infer dispersal patterns, while describing genetic diversity will allow to inform appropriate measures to preserve it. To fill this knowledge gap, we used a genetic multi-marker approach. We evaluated population structure and assessed connectivity at different spatial scales – from ocean basins to the island groups within the Azores archipelago - through the analysis of Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) markers and Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). The results of this project will provide science-based knowledge to support suitable management and conservation actions, regionally and globally.
keywords: Mobula; Genetics; Connectivity; Population structure; Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms

title: Small-scale fishers are incentivised to overfish threatened sharks and exacerbate their own vulnerability
abstract_text: To achieve sustainable shark fisheries, it is as important to understand the social and economic drivers of overfishing as it is the biological drivers and environmental consequences. The extinction risk of sharks is disproportionately higher in coastal tropical waters where small-scale fisheries dominate, presenting unique management challenges. Small-scale fisheries provide a critical source of economic and nutritional security, but fishers are among the most vulnerable socio-economic groups because their exposure to economic, social, and environmental shocks is combined with limited adaptive capacity. Using Kenya and Zanzibar as a case study, we examine the interactions between sharks and small-scale fisheries. We find that sharks are an important source of economic and nutritional security, primarily from species threatened with extinction. Further, the most economically valuable sharks are larger, slower reproducing, and more likely to be threatened with extinction, providing a strong economic incentive to target endangered species. Given the high economic motivation and intensive fishing pressure, small-scale fisheries are undoubtedly important contributors to the ongoing decline of many threatened shark species. The decline of sharks may have damaging consequences for wider marine ecosystems and ecosystem services. In the absence of effective fisheries management, we show that within small-scale fisheries the conditions exist for an economically incentivised positive feedback loop in which vulnerable fishers are driven to persistently overfish vulnerable and declining resources. In doing so, they undermine their own economic and nutritional security and that of their communities. To be successful management must break the feedback loop or be doomed to failure.
keywords: fisheries; endangered species; food security; nutrition; economics

title: Eco-responsible research vessel : Parsifal
abstract_text: Against a context of global change, the world is facing new challenges. This is the backdrop to our project to build an eco-responsible research vessel called the Parsifal. For over 2 years, the members of our team have been renovating this boat with the aim of making it an ambassador for sharks. The ultimate goal is to navigate all around the world using La Pérouse's route, while carrying out a range of scientific studies. This boat will enable us to carry out a wide range of projects on sharks in remote areas, focusing on conservation issues, studies and surveys in isolated areas for example. Shark diving, water sampling and fisheries data collection will all be part of the programme. Our expeditions will be accompanied by scientific documentaries to show the reality of shark science to people who are not involved in this field, thus highlighting the different players at sea. The aim of this eco-responsible vessel is to play an active role in the study and conservation of sharks around the world. Various scientists from all around the world, studying different aspects of sharks, will be presented and they will be invited to collaborate with our work to carry out expeditions and take samples throughout the expeditions.

title: Monitoring the development of Nursehound Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758) (Chondrichthyes: Scyliorhinidae) eggcases in-situ
abstract_text: The Nursehound Scyliorhinus stellaris (Linnaeus, 1758) is a medium-sized catshark that resides in the Northeast Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea. It is classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (Near Threatened under the European and Mediterranean assessments) and although distribution is patchy, they can be locally abundant. This oviparous species occurs on the continental and insular shelf, generally inhabiting shallow coastal waters where they have been documented depositing their eggs. The curled tendrils extending from the capsule are used to anchor the eggcase to a substrate while the embryo develops over an incubation period of approximately 9 – 11 months. A sheltered channel was discovered in south Devon (southwest England) where Nursehounds were consistently depositing their eggs, usually attached to the algae Rainbow Wrack Ericaria selaginoides (Linnaeus) Molinari & Guiry, 2020. Accessible by snorkelling on a low spring tide, this site has been visited on a regular basis (once to twice a month) since April 2014 to monitor developing eggcases, assess the level of biofouling, and document freshly deposited eggcases. To date, 326 eggcases have been recorded at this site (average 36 per year), with 159 having been seen consistently from deposition through to hatching, others have been predated upon or have washed away during storms. The goal of this citizen science project is to determine the average development period in order to gain further insight on the species in the wild and gain a greater understanding of egg deposition in this species.

title: 20 years of citizen science - the Great Eggcase Hunt
abstract_text: The Great Eggcase Hunt is a citizen science initiative that was established by the Shark Trust in 2003. Over the last 20 years, the project has received ~25,000 submissions from ~13,000 participants, (although this figure represents far greater pool of participants from group events) totalling over 440,000 eggcases from 46 oviparous elasmobranch species around the world. Although the majority of data is from the British Isles, where the project was established, the Great Eggcase Hunt receives submissions from around the world. Multiple identification guides have been created in collaboration with regional organisations (i.e. Turkey, Portugal and Australia), along with development of a citizen science mobile app. Analysis of this dataset can be used to pick out temporal and seasonal patterns: It can allow hotpots for eggcases to be identified – signifying potential egglaying grounds - as well as highlighting locations that are lacking in records and may require more searching effort. Data submitted from regular reporters allow for a finer scale understanding of seasonality of eggcase finds, with regular reporters spread across the UK allowing comparison. Data from the Great Eggcase Hunt has led to an improved understanding of eggcase morphology (e.g., the Common Skate complex) and can even be used to help identify possible spawning grounds. As well as species-specific data, a dataset of this size provides a valuable insight into citizen science engagement, including the growth of the project in terms of both numbers (of participants and eggcase finds) and spread of engagement, along with the seasonality of reporting.

title: Biting off more than we can chew: DNA barcoding reveals patterns of species utilisation, threatened species and mislabelling in shark products across Europe
abstract_text: The global shark trade plays a major role in the exploitation of shark populations. Multiple studies have uncovered fraud in European shark meat markets, including sales of prohibited and threatened species, and high levels of mislabelling. However, to date, few have assessed large-scale patterns across multiple countries. Combining samples collected by citizen science projects and NGOs with data from a systematic meta-analysis, this study investigated a total of 792 shark products identified using DNA barcoding, across ten countries: Greece, Italy, UK, Spain, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Austria and Iceland; and four retailer types: fish markets, fishmongers, processed products and supermarkets. The blue shark (Prionace glauca), listed as critically endangered in the Mediterranean, was the most identified species in the study, especially among Mediterranean countries. Furthermore, the results indicate significant differences in species utilisation across countries, potentially influenced by geographic proximity to different fisheries. Worryingly, vulnerable species were found on sale in all countries and retailer types in the study. Mislabelling rates were relatively high (32.4%), potentially driven by the opportunistic use of threatened species from bycatch. Overall, the study highlights the need for improved implementation of management and labelling legislation to enable more informed consumer choices and to reduce the overexploitation of shark populations.

title: Stakeholder engagement as key tool for elasmobranch conservation in the Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: In the Mediterranean Sea, more than 40% of the assessed chondrichthyan species are considered threatened. In addition, there are two other complexity factors that make the conservation challenge more difficult and increase the risk of extinction of cartilaginous fishes: 1) elasmobranchs pass through multiple jurisdictions with different fishery and environmental regulations; 2) sharks and their relatives also have different social and economic considerations, serving in some cases as subsistence for communities. In this controversial scenario, where common environmental policy actions are really difficult, marine stakeholders can play a key role to start a concrete conservation of marine biodiversity, especially for organisms still considered dangerous, like sharks and their relatives. The LIFE ELIFE project (LIFE18 NAT/IT/000846), co-funded by the EU LIFE programme, includes two conservation actions focused on the awareness and the engagememt of citizens and stakeholders, in order to increase their attention on the great vulnerability of these animals. In this framework, here we report four recent best practice events for the conservation of elasmobranchs, carried out by common citizens and professional fishers, allowing the survival of 2 manta rays (Mobula mobular), one blue shark (Prionace glauca) and one angel shark (Squatina sp.). The success of these initiatives was based on the strong voluntary collaboration among several actors (citizens, scientists, fishers, authorities, MPAs) and it highlights how their engagement can be the real key tool to carry out concrete actions aimed to elasmobranch conservation in the Mediterranean Sea, anticipating common political steps.

title: Sussex IFCA Elasmobranch Code of Conduct
abstract_text: Many species of elasmobranchs are overfished, and populations have declined substantially, both internationally and within UK waters, including in Sussex. Research indicates that the majority of elasmobranchs landed in trawl fisheries in the English Channel are below their L50, and therefore likely before they have reproduced. This suggests size-based management, which aims to increase the proportion of individuals that are harvested post-reproductive age therefore increasing recruitment and population growth, is appropriate in Sussex. The conservation challenges faced by elasmobranchs include their tendency to be caught as bycatch, however commercial fishers are constrained by quota restrictions on skate and ray species (certain species are aggregated into a single term 'Skates and Rays). Recreational fishers are not always subject to the same restrictions as commercial fishers and are more likely to be receptive to voluntary measures. Therefore, to promote sustainable fishing practices amongst local anglers, Sussex Inshore Fisheries and Conservation Authority (IFCA) developed a voluntary code of conduct that details recommended minimum landing sizes, a welfare guide, and a concise location-specific ID guide. It is also intended to help commercial fishers engage in more conservation-orientated behaviours regarding how elasmobranch bycatch is processed. Minimum sizes were selected based on a literature review used to calculate the average size at which 50% of the population has reached sexual maturity (L50), and the most threatened and least protected species were considered priorities for inclusion in the code of conduct. Sussex IFCA plan to publish this code of conduct alongside confirmation of broader sized based management within the district.

title: Multidisciplinary approach to study the interaction and survival of pelagic shark in recreational fisheries in the Northern Adriatic Sea
abstract_text: Recreational fisheries in the Northern Adriatic Sea consist of a range of fishing techniques targeting several species (Pranovi et al., 2016). Drifting is one of the most commnly used methods, employed especially for catch and release (C&R) fishing of Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus). The fishery is also known to accidentally catch pelagic shark species, though the species composition, seasonality, and potential impact of the fishery on the shark assemblage in the region is poorly understood. In the last four years, logbook data was collected in collaboration with nearly 20 drifting fishers to assess the by-catch rate and area of occurrence of three neritic sharks. Among these species, the blue shark (Prionace glauca) is the most frequently caught, followed by the common thresher shark (Alopias vulpinus) and the sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus). Questionnaires were also used to gather local ecological knowledge (LEK) regarding the by-catch rate, area of seasonal occurrence, age composition, and post-release survival perception for the three species. Finally, post-release survival of these species is being assessed through the deployment of a combination of conventional (spaghetti tag), acoustic (sentinel array of 18 VR2tX receivers and V13 transmitters by Innovasea) and satellite (sPAT) tagging. This multidisciplinary approach has the potential to contribute to closing the knowledge gap on the movement ecology of these species in the Northern Adriatic Sea, while also helping to quantify the potential impact of drifting fishing on shark populations.

title: Metabolic enzyme activity in Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) tissue at varying temperatures and age
abstract_text: The Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus) is the longest living vertebrate with a lifespan of multiple centuries. We investigated the activity of metabolic enzymes related to fatty acid oxidation and anaerobic metabolism in animals 200–434cm in length (~age range of 60-200 years) to determine variation with age. We investigated red muscle (RM; n=23) and liver (n=13). Enzyme assays were run in triplicate at two temperatures, 21oC and ∼5oC (mean±SEM). Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity saw no variation with age and was higher in RM when measured under cold conditions (32.08 ± 3.1U/g tissue) in comparison to warm conditions (10.48 ± 0.74U/g tissue). A similar temperature trend was seen in liver tissue with LDH assayed at cold temperatures (17.89 ± 1.83U/g tissue/min) being greater than warm temperatures (3.54 ± 0.91U/g tissue). Higher LDH activity under colder conditions may suggests cold-water adaptations to bolster LDH activity in Greenland sharks, as seen in some polar fish. 3-Hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (HOAD) showed no significant variation between cold (4.47 ± 0.68U/g tissue) and warm (6.25 ± 1.42U/g tissue) assays in the liver of sharks. HOAD activity in RM was lower under cold (3.95 ± 0.47U/g tissue) than in warm assays (13.65 ± 1.68U/g tissue). Greenland shark HOAD activity has an opposing trend to temperate sharks, which in past literature shows greater HOAD activity in the liver than RM. We have shown that Greenland shark metabolism displays unique specialisations in comparison to other elasmobranchs and shows possible enzymatic adaptations to polar environments, which may be associated with their remarkable longevity.

title: What do you want for dinner? Sharks and Rays' diets in Amvrakikos Gulf (Greece)
abstract_text: Stomach content analysis provides insights into elasmobranchs feeding patterns, food habits, and ecological role. Moreover, it is fundamental in the development of ecosystem-based management approaches. This study is using stomach content analysis to understand the feeding ecology of demersal elasmobranchs, in particular 6 rays and 1 shark. The study area, the Amvrakikos Gulf, is a semi-enclosed embayment of approximately 400 km2 located in the north-western Greece, characterised by shallow waters, muddy bottom, high freshwater influx and seasonal hypoxia and anoxia. Only small-scale fishery is operating within the Gulf. In the contest of the By ElasmoCatch Project, a total of 293 stomachs were collected from dead individuals, either bycaught or targeted by the fishing activities. From 2022 up to now stomach contents of 37 Aetomylaeus bovinus, 146 Dasyatis spp., 37 Gymnura altavela, 36 Mustelus mustelus, 7 Myliobatis aquila and 30 Torpedo torpedo have been analysed. Specifically, we are investigating: (i) species-specific diet preferences; (ii) degree of diet overlap among species; (iii) size and sex-related variability in diet. All preys were identified to the lowest taxonomical level possible. Decapoda, Bivalvia and Clupeidae constituted the main prey items recorded in the stomachs. Future studies will include metabarcoding of stomach contents of elasmobranchs with non-invasive methods (e.g., anal swabs) to integrate data coming from stable isotope analyses (biopsies) and traditional stomach content analysis. In addition, higher sample size is needed to further investigate changes in diets and the spatial coverage of the feeding grounds inside the Amvrakikos Gulf.

title: Solving the riddle: insights on species-specific identification for individuals of the family Dasyatidae
abstract_text: Species-specific identification is of fundamental importance in determining the quantitative composition of bycatch and associated mortality. Biological and ecological knowledge is mostly needed at the species level to build effective management strategies that can improve the poor conservation status of Chondrichthyes in the Mediterranean Sea. Within the several species of the family Dasyatidae, some are characterised by similar morphological traits, especially in the juvenile stages. For example, Dasyatis tortonesei has been only recently recognised as different in respect to Dasyatis pastinaca, based on some differences in colours, morphology, and teeth. Among the stingrays which are commonly bycaught by the small-scale fishery in Amvrakikos Gulf (Greece), there are individuals of the family Dasyatidae, in particular 3 species: Bathytoshia lata, D. pastinaca and D. tortonesei. The aim of this study is to find practical identification keys to classify every specimen at the species level, solving ambiguities in the whole Mediterranean Sea. A total of 310 samples were collected from February 2022 until now. One or two photos (dorsally and ventrally) were taken respectively in alive (N = 126) and dead animals (N = 184). Morphometric measures were obtained through ImageJ Software. Moreover, in dead animals, DNA samples were collected to compare morphometry to genetic identification. title: Documenting a unknown Nearshore aggregation area for the Blackchin Guitarfish Glaucostegus cemiculus in Turkey
abstract_text: In 2005 a guitarfish aggregations in shallow waters was documented in a small bay on the Turkish Aegean coast, Eastern Mediterranean sea. Visual surveys were conducted, which allowed the documentation of guitarfish presence, estimated total length 150-170cm, and which was not available from data based on fishery catches. The census took place during 2005 and 2006, and the presence of sharks has been reconfirmed in 2023. The identification of aggregation areas plays a crucial role in the conservation of species such as the black guitarfish, which was historically common throughout the Mediterranean Sea but has now disappeared from the northern parts of its range. Available data suggest that the black guitarfish has suffered a population decline of >80% in the last three generations (45 years) and is considered critically endangered.

title: EU Sharks LIFE
abstract_text: LIFE EUSharks (LIFE22-GIE-IT-101114031), is a Project funded by the European Commission's LIFE programme, and for the next 4 years, it will actively engage European citizens and marine stakeholders in a common effort to preserve sharks and rays in Italy, France, Croatia, Spain and Slovenia (i.e. in the Mediterranean subregions where has been recorded the largest decline of elasmobranchs). LIFE EUSharks aims to identify behavioural changes, rather than technical ones, to reduce the anthropogenic impact on biodiversity: it will remove the knowledge barriers that hinder the implementation of the EU regulations designed to protect sharks, and it will promote active stakeholder and citizen engagement: EUSharks will give strength to sustainable commercial and recreational fishing and local seafood consumption. Moreover, it will increase the stakeholders and public's understanding of the essential role of these charismatic and endangered species in the Mediterranean ecosystems. The project's strategy is to address the Mediterranean elasmobranch decline with a participatory approach, promoting behavioural change and fostering co-responsibility as key drivers. It will initiate and strengthen institutional and professional relationships and will ensure the engagement of all actors in supporting best practices beyond the project's lifetime. title: Bringing up baby: shark young life stages and our warming oceans
abstract_text: While climate change is predicted to have unprecedented impacts on marine fish biological organization, the responses of elasmobranchs have rarely been studied, despite the threat it may add to direct anthropogenic pressures such as overfishing and habitat degradation. Here, we assessed the impact of warming and acidification under the climate scenarios SSP2: Middle of the road and SSP5: Fossil-fueled Development (Taking the Highway) for the 21st century on the growth, survival and metabolism of embryos and juveniles of a model species for the Northeast Atlantic: the Small-spotted Catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula). Specifically, as physiological processes are limited by a precise thermal range, we used for the first time monthly temperature variations rather than an annual average. This experimental set-up revealed the high vulnerability of embryos to extreme summer temperatures, with hatching success ranging from 82% for the control and SSP2-4.5 treatment to only 15% for the SSP5-8.5 treatment. More specifically, growth trajectories revealed that SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 embryos progressively diverged from control embryos, but that only SSP2-4.5 embryos managed to reduce this gap, with SSP5-8.5 embryos dying in their 5th stage of development. Embryos with the lowest hatching success were distinguished by lower yolk consumption rates, lower growth rates and higher energy demands. Within 6 months after hatching, we did not observe any additional mortality, but we detected a higher growth rate in SSP5-8.5 juveniles. Ultimately, we estimated that an intermediate scenario for the 21st century could lead to a survival rate of young life stages similar to the current rate, while a fossil fuel-based development scenario could lead to a disruption of population dynamics due to very high embryonic mortality.
keywords: climate change; sharks; embryo

title: Movegroup: an R package to calculate and visualise space use and home range for groups of animals
abstract_text: Calculating home ranges is a common task for spatial analysis of sharks, typically producing contours containing 50 and 95% of their space use, which can inform MPA selection and reveal habitat preferences. Improving on the original Minimum Convex Polygon approach, the kernel utilization distribution (KUD) approach added the intensity of subarea use, which was itself bettered by the Brownian bridge movement model (BBMM) approach, which models movements between subsequent relocations explicitly, translating animal movement speed into between-point variance. Dynamic Brownian bridge movement models (dBBMM) refine this further by allowing this variance (spatial error) to change along a movement trajectory, improving performance, especially for irregular tracks (e.g. satellite tag data). dBBMM space use can be calculated for a single animal using the move package, however this is unsuitable for multiple individuals, for a few reasons. Firstly, it requires a continuous chronological record, but multiple individuals will likely overlap in time. Second, individuals' data are typically unequal in space and time: some tags stay on longer, some individuals travel further. These sampling imbalances would invalidate group-level space-use calculations. Movegroup allows multiple individuals, using scaling to ensure biologically accurate results, and unbalanced receiver arrays can be easily accommodated. Movegroup automates the typical workflow, scaling and reprojecting multiple tracks to the same projection and extent, plotting rich output maps, and saving space use and variance calculations. The package is well documented, and is available on GitHub now, and CRAN soon.
keywords: Home range; space use; dBBMM; KUD; movement

title: Fishing Metallomic Signatures of Extreme Longevity in the Greenland shark
abstract_text: Most metallomics studies focusing on non-model organisms have interpreted metal accumulation within the scope of ecology, but recent evidence suggests that the metallome can also inform us about other biological aspects of wild species. Metallomics in relation to physiology is an emerging approach, which enables tissue metal concentrations to be linked to biological processes, such as ageing. Using inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), we examined the metallomes of the heart ventricle, heart atrium, red muscle, white muscle, spleen, and liver in the world's longest-lived vertebrate, the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus). As previous studies have shown, we confirm tissue-specific elemental concentration patterns, and we propose that these differences reflect tissue function. Across tissues, age-dependent metallomic changes involved a few essential (Ca, Fe, Na, Se, and Zn) and non-essential elements (As, Cd, and Pb). However, bivariate analysis suggested that these age-associated changes could relate to interactions between essential elements and the accumulation of heavy metals (especially Pb) rather than an effect of ageing per se. Then, we compared the heart metallome of the Greenland shark with that of other shorter-lived vertebrate species. We found that heart concentrations of essential elements (Cu, K, Fe, Mg, Mn, and Mo), especially Cu, and Fe levels were lower in the Greenland shark relative to mouse, sheep, human, and the small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula), which is interesting as these elements are known to be more concentrated in senescent cells, and might also correlate with metabolic rate. In contrast, cardiac Se and As levels were higher in the Greenland shark compared with the other vertebrates, perhaps suggesting enhanced antioxidative capabilities. Together, these data indicate that the metallomic landscape of the Greenland shark is subjected to only minor changes with age, and that its longevity may benefit from properties associated with mitochondrial function.
keywords: Metallomics; ICP-MS; Ageing; Longevity; Greenland shark

title: A field lab for concrete management and conservation of elasmobranchs in the Mediterranean Sea: the Marine Protected Area of Egadi Islands
abstract_text: Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) can significantly contribute to the conservation of marine ecosystem by safeguarding habitats, reducing fishing pressure, promoting population recovery, supporting scientific research, raising public awareness, generating economic benefits and fostering collaboration among various stakeholders. Despite their relevance, the benefits that MPAs can bring for sharks and their relatives is still debated and little known, mainly in the Mediterranean Sea. Since 2021, a multidisciplanary monitoring programme on elasmobranchs in the largest MPA of the Mediterranean basin, located in the Egadi islands, has recorded the catch of 200 elasmobranchs of 5 different species. Adult sharks of genus Mustelus are the most abundant catch: they are regularly landed, representing a remarkable local economic resource. On the contrary, several releases carried out by fishers of juveniles of Mustelus mustelus, Mustelus punctulatus and Myliobatis aquila were also recorded. Interviews based on a focused LEK (Local Ecological Knownledge) protocol were also conducted with local fishers with more than 25 years of professional experience, which revealed a permanent presence of elasmobranchs in the area, constant in species composition and with no remarkable decrease. Our preliminary results show that a strong collaboration, dialogue and trust among different stakeholders (officers, fishers, authorities, scientists) in a MPA can also provide good management and conservation for elasmobranchs, with direct environmental and socio-economic benefits. In this framework, MPAs can serve as natural filed lab to collect long-term data and testing new solutions to reduce human impact on cartilaginous fish, like innovative fishing gears.
keywords: MPAs; LEK; Mediterranean

title: Occurrence of trophically-transmitted nematodes including anisakid larvae in seven species of Rajidae from English Channel and Celtic Sea
abstract_text: As part of an overall study on the parasitofauna of elasmobranches in North-East Atlantic, we researched nematodes in 114 skates belonging to seven Rajiidae species (9 Leucoraja fullonica, 15 Leucoraja naevus, 21 Raja brachyura, 20 Raja clavata, 14 Raja microocellata, 21 Raja montagui, and 14 Raja undulata). Among the metazoan parasite taxa found (helminths and Myxosporea), nematodes were the most prevalent infecting 37% (CL 29-46%) of the skates with mean abundance and intensity of respectively 1.6 1.2 and 11.5 4.0 worms per skate. Whatever the skate species, its community of metazoan parasites was always dominated by nematodes. Four species of nematodes were identified through DNA-sequencing: Anisakis simplex s.s., Proleptus sp., Pseudoterranova arasi and Pseudoterranova krabbei. It was a first record for A. simplex s.s. in L. fullonica, Proleptus sp. in R. brachyura, and Pseudoterranova spp. in L. fullonica, L. naevus, R. microocellata, R. montagui and R. undulata. The dominant metazoan parasites were, in decreasing order, Pseudoterranova spp., Proleptus sp. and A. simplex, each taxon encountered in five of the seven skate species. Information provided by trophically-transmitted nematodes on skates confirmed their opportunistic diet based on crustaceans (intermediate hosts) and teleosts (paratenic hosts, also including cephalopods). The occurrence of Pseudoterranova spp. and A. simplex may confirm the worldwide increase of anisakiasis and raises the question of anisakiasis risk for human consumption. Further research is needed on the role of Rajidae in the anisakid transmission to mammal definitive hosts (seals and cetaceans) as only seals are known to prey skates.

title: Striving for good science - An Early Career Scientists' perspective on animal welfare considerations in elasmobranch telemetry
abstract_text: Recent advancements in electronic tracking devices have revolutionized the study of species' movements, behaviour, and physiology in the past decade. During the same time, countries have enacted regulations to ensure animal welfare within research, which focuses on laboratory-based research. Field-based research, such as that involved in telemetry studies, has to adhere to the same regulations. However, we see a gap in how classical principles fundamental to animal welfare in research can be applied to this field. This poster seeks to present a comprehensive approach to enhance animal welfare and scientific practices in elasmobranch telemetry studies, guided by the Three R's principles: Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement. It highlights key considerations within each dimension while critically reflecting on associated issues and opportunities, such as the potential for collecting complementary data, facilitating data access, and nurturing a culture of data, knowledge, and capacity sharing across boundaries and generations. Through this, we aim to emphasize the relevance of elasmobranch welfare within research, encourage a more critical assessment and reflection of the welfare issues involved, and ultimately strive for better science as a whole as part of the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development.
keywords: Animal welfare; Perspective; Elasmobranch telemetry; Tagging; Three Rs

title: Genetic monitoring of the critically endangered flapper skate in a Northeast Atlantic Marine Protected Area
abstract_text: Declines in the critically endangered flapper skate (Dipturus intermedius) in the Northeast Atlantic (NEA) prompted designation of a marine protected area (MPA) 'Loch Sunart to the Sound of Jura' (LSSJ) on the Scottish west coast. Tagging studies in this area had shown high levels of site affinity supporting the move for spatial protection but whether such spatial management would benefit other NEA populations was unknown. An ideal MPA should sustain a viable population that shows some connectivity, replenishing others through spillover. Mitochondrial DNA analyses revealed the LSSJ MPA has low genetic diversity and restricted connectivity compared to other NEA populations, raising fears about potential inbreeding within the most protected flapper skate population. Here we used >4,800 genome-wide Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) to gain more insight into nuclear diversity and geneflow between the MPA and other populations. The LSSJ MPA had a reassuring degree of nuclear genetic diversity but remained significantly genetically differentiated from other populations. Further, high levels of close kin were observed in the MPA, confirming a generally low dispersal rate, with relatives remaining almost exclusively in a relatively short distance from each other. Hence, while the LSSJ MPA protects genetic diversity, there is limited outgoing gene flow and a low number of breeders, implying it is unlikely to replenish less protected populations from spillover. To enable further genetic monitoring of the MPA and other flapper skate populations, we are establishing reduced SNP panels using rapid real-time PCR assays to identify individuals though genetic tagging.

title: Are small scale fishers interacting with elasmobranchs in the Canary Islands?
abstract_text: Interactions between fauna and fisheries are a worldwide problem, occurring also in the Canary Islands. These islands are characterised by a multi-specific artisanal fishing fleet that plays a major role in the food security of the archipelago, as well as being of economic and cultural value. On the other hand, the archipelago holds a rich marine biodiversity, including 93 condrictian species. Elasmobranchs are not a predominant target group of fisheries here, catches being mainly of dogfish and blue sharks. The range areas of elasmobranch species overlap with fishing grounds, sharing in some cases the interest in a common resource. This facilitates the appearance of human-wildlife interactions, which can be positive or negative. Negative interactions may compromise species conservation (bycatch, intentional killing, changes in distribution and diet) and have a social and economic impact (capture loss, gear damage, reduction of the CPUE). The aim of this study is to obtain the first archipelagic characterization of the interactions between the small-scale fisheries and elasmobranchs in the Canary Islands. A total of 235 interviews were conducted in 25 fishers' guilds to assess the typology, intensity, losses, mitigation measures and fishers' perception. Depredation and gear damage interactions by sharks and rays were reported by 69.4% and 28.9% of interviewees respectively, involving 21 elasmobranch species. 66% and 67.2% of interviewees reported having accidentally caught at least one shark or ray during their careers respectively. A better understanding of the interactions and correct management tools can improve the coexistence and sustainability of small-scale fisheries.
keywords: human-wildlife interactions; fisheries; depredation; bycatch; elasmobranchs

title: Assessing the impact of regulations on the manta and devil ray gill plate trade
abstract_text: Many populations of manta and devil rays (mobulids) around the world are in steep decline, primarily due to overfishing. Caught as bycatch in non-selective gear, or purposefully targeted, the primary financial driver for their demise is the trade in their gill plates. Mobulid gill plates are purported as Traditional Chinese Medicines (TCM). They are traded internationally from source countries and sent to mainland China primarily as well as other locations despite CITES trade regulations being in place since 2013 (for mantas) and 2016 (for devil rays). Here, we assess the effectiveness of regulating international trade in manta and devil ray gill plates through listing of these species on Appendix II of CITES, to identify key drivers of this trade at the level of source, re-export, and sink countries. By collecting and comparing market, online, and official trade data, we determine impacts of the CITES Appendix II listings and assess their effectiveness. We collected market data in Guangzhou on the quantities of gill plates sold, their cost, stated country of origin, and the accessibility to customers. Additionally, because the last few years have seen a growth in online trading, we complement this market data with information on gill plates sold on online markets and platforms. Finally, we assess trends in the gill plate trade based on surveys conducted over the past decade and discuss further steps to bring to quantify the mismatch between exports and imports of gills globally.

title: Genetic structure and demographic analysis of the undulate skates Raja undulata from the Northeast Atlantic Ocean
abstract_text: It is crucial to regularly evaluate the genetic diversity and structure of endangered species. This is particularly important in elasmobranchs given their life strategy, which increases their vulnerability to overexploitation, in order to delineate and improve their management and conservation. The undulate ray, Raja undulata, is a skate distributed along the northeast coast of the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea that exhibits patchy distributions across continental shelves. Currently, undulate rays are catalogued as Endangered by the IUCN, with a decreasing population trend, rendering it crucial to improve their management. The aim of this study was to assess the diversity and genetic structure in Northeast Atlantic Ocean populations of Raja undulata. Samples were collected via non-invasive mucus swabs by qualified scuba divers between 2017 – 2018, with microsatellites from a total of 137 individuals being successfully amplified from 10 species-specific loci. Global genetic diversity levels were high among localities (Ho=0.757). Genetic structure analysis suggests panmixia along the coast of the Northeast Atlantic Ocean (FST=0.029; p>0.05), which may be promoted by the high connectivity between localities. Due to the lack of differentiation among localities, we calculate a single effective population size (Ne) of 102.7 which, according with the IUCN criteria, it is sufficient to avoid inbreeding depression but concerning to maintain evolutionary potential. These panmixia findings highlight the significance of continuing to research migratory patterns in order to clarify the factors that promote population homogenization.
